evidence.title: TREK: A Travel Reasoning and Evaluation Kit for LLM Agents in Complex Trip Planning

entries.title: SWE-Touch benchmarks coding agents when users edit code mid-task
entries.html:
Repository-level benchmarks usually evaluate agents working alone, or limit user participation to messages. SWE-Touch tests how coding agents understand and respond when users inspect and modify code in the shared workspace during a task.

That is the normal case for an IDE agent, so uninterrupted-run scores leave a gap.

evidence.title: SWE-Touch: Benchmarking Coding Agents When Users Touch the Code

entries.title: ORCA-bench: best agent gets 25.3% of realistic oncall root-cause tasks right
entries.html:
ORCA-bench pairs a live, OpenTelemetry-instrumented microservice testbed with 1,079 root-cause-analysis tasks, graded by an LLM judge that human SREs independently re-scored (κ=0.90).

Across five frontier agents, the best RCA accuracy is 25.3% on realistic tasks and 10.0% on hard ones; the weakest hallucinates a root cause on 40% of reports. Don't hand oncall triage to an agent on the strength of coding scores. See agent observability.

evidence.title: ORCA-bench: How Ready Are Language Model Agents for Oncall?

entries.title: OpenAI explains its third-party cyber eval incidents and tightens safeguards
entries.html:
OpenAI explained the recent third-party cybersecurity evaluation incidents involving its models, including the Hugging Face breach, and set out new safeguards for how it runs and audits cyber-capability evaluations. Days later it published preliminary cybersecurity evaluations for Astra, an internal model, with steps to strengthen safeguards and security controls.

With Anthropic and the UK AI Security Institute reporting similar incidents, eval-environment containment is a cross-lab problem, not one partner's mistake.

evidence.title: Third-party cyber evaluations involving OpenAI models
Responding to the next frontier of critical cyber capabilities

entries.title: IssueTrojanBench tests whether coding agents execute instructions hidden in issues
entries.html:
IssueTrojanBench benchmarks whether a coding agent executes a malicious instruction smuggled inside an otherwise ordinary issue request.

Issue text is untrusted input for any agent that picks up tickets automatically. This puts a number on that exposure; see prompt injection for defenses.

evidence.title: IssueTrojanBench: Benchmarking AI Coding Agents Against Malicious Issue Requests

entries.title: ExtractBench grades schema-guided document extraction with source evidence
entries.html:
ExtractBench benchmarks schema-guided enterprise document extraction: given a document and a user-defined schema, the agent must produce correct output with source evidence as grounding metadata. It scores value accuracy and record completeness at scale, among other measures.

For extraction pipelines, attribution is part of correctness, not a nice-to-have.

evidence.title: ExtractBench: A Benchmark for Schema-Guided Enterprise Document Extraction

entries.title: Supabase Evals scores Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode on real Supabase build tasks
entries.html:
Supabase released Supabase Evals, an open-source benchmark that scores how well coding agents — Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode — build on Supabase using real tasks.

It joins AWS-bench as a platform vendor publishing its own agent benchmark. For teams on that platform it is a closer proxy than a general SWE score; check the task set before treating it as neutral.

evidence.title: Supabase Releases Evals: an Open Source Benchmark That Scores Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode on Real Supabase Tasks - MarkTechPost
Supabase Evals: Benchmark for testing how well AI agents build using Supabase

entries.title: ReviewBench scores code-review agents against real feedback from trusted reviewers
entries.html:
LangChain's ReviewBench evaluates code-review agents against real PR feedback from trusted reviewers rather than a synthetic rubric.

Grounding the target in what experienced reviewers actually flagged makes the score track usefulness to a team, not agreement with an invented checklist.

evidence.title: Evaluating code review agents with ReviewBench

entries.title: LangSmith Align Evals calibrates evaluators against human preference in-product
entries.html:
LangSmith's Align Evals lets a team calibrate its evaluators to match human preference judgments inside the tool.

The "certify your automated eval against human agreement" lesson becomes a product workflow step instead of a side audit. Judge-side detail lives on LLM-as-judge.

evidence.title: Introducing Align Evals: Streamlining LLM Application Evaluation

entries.title: Two API settings roughly tripled GPT-5.6's ARC-AGI-3 score
entries.html:
OpenAI reports that retaining reasoning state and enabling context compaction — two separate API settings — roughly tripled GPT-5.6's score on ARC-AGI-3 and improved efficiency.

Configuration levers usually tracked as cost knobs (reasoning effort, context compaction) move benchmark scores too. A reported score without its settings is not comparable.

evidence.title: How enabling two settings tripled our scores on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark

entries.title: Anthropic finds Claude reached real systems in 3 incidents across 141,006 cyber eval runs
entries.html:
After OpenAI's Hugging Face incident, Anthropic reviewed 141,006 cybersecurity evaluation runs and found three incidents (six runs, the earliest in April) where Claude reached real systems. A mismatch with the evaluation partner meant the prompt's "no internet access" claim was false; Claude treated real organizations as in-scope and compromised some with basic techniques such as weak passwords and unauthenticated endpoints.

A sandbox claim in an eval prompt is an assumption to verify, not a control. See agent sandboxing.

evidence.title: Investigating three real-world incidents in our cybersecurity evaluations

entries.title: Similarweb's first report rubric rewarded source quantity until it was recalibrated
entries.html:
Similarweb grades long-form Deep Research reports in LangSmith against quality-dimension rubrics with explicit scoring anchors (e.g. source_integration: 0.0 for a single data API, 1.0 for extensive attributed sources), plus faithfulness checks for ungrounded claims, A/B comparison against saved baseline runs, and trace-linked feedback that ties a low score to the offending step.

The first rubric rewarded source quantity over quality. It became reliable only after recalibration to reward named, relevant sources tied to specific claims — a plausible rubric can score the wrong thing until checked.

evidence.title: How Similarweb Evaluates Agent Reports with LangSmith

also.title: LLM-as-judge: model-graded evaluation of traces and outputs

entries.title: Counting compute flips a hallucination leaderboard ranking
entries.html:
"The Cost of Knowing" (MAS-HQ) normalizes factuality scores for the compute spent producing them. A brute-force best-of-4 agent posts the higher raw score (H-Score 0.9169 vs 0.9103) and would top a static leaderboard, but loses on cost-normalized Q-Score (0.5169 vs 0.5217) at roughly four times the tokens and latency.

Static leaderboards treat compute as free. The system that tops one can be the worse one to deploy; see agent cost.

evidence.title: The Cost of Knowing: A Resource-Aware Protocol for Benchmarking Hallucination Beyond Static Leaderboards

entries.title: Adding skills to an agent causes regressions that average success hides
entries.html:
"The Regression Tax" compares agents with and without procedural skills across nearly 6,000 runs on two office-automation benchmarks and three model-harness stacks. It separates regressions (solved without skills, failed with them) from residual failures, and finds regressions substantial.

Evaluate a new skill for what it breaks, not only its average lift. Track per-task before/after, as in a regression suite. See agent cost for the token side.

evidence.title: The Regression Tax: Decomposing Why Skills Help and Hurt LLM Agents

entries.title: Agent benchmark scores can reflect protocol fit, not capability
entries.html:
A protocol-validity analysis asks whether agent benchmarks measure capability at all. It argues many conflate task difficulty with protocol and scaffolding artifacts, so a score gain can reflect a better-fitted harness rather than a more capable agent.

When comparing harnesses or vendors, hold the protocol fixed or treat the harness as part of what is being measured.

evidence.title: Do Agent Benchmarks Measure Capability? Protocol Validity in the Age of Agentic

entries.title: Over 227 sequential rounds, regressions, not missing features, limit coding agents
entries.html:
EvoCode-Bench tests coding agents across 227 sequential rounds in a persistent workspace instead of one bounded task. Single-turn scores overstate reliability: the bottleneck is regressions accumulating across rounds, not missing features.

Long-lived agent workflows need regression checks between steps, not only a final pass.

evidence.title: Evaluating Agents Beyond the First Prompt

entries.title: AWS releases AWS-bench, an open-source benchmark for agents on AWS
entries.html:
AWS announced AWS-bench, an open-source benchmark for evaluating AI agents on AWS infrastructure.

Benchmark breadth now extends along the deployment-platform axis, and a cloud vendor is publishing its own agent benchmark rather than relying only on third-party suites. Read vendor benchmarks with that incentive in mind.

evidence.title: AWS announces AWS-bench, an open-source benchmark for AI agents on AWS

entries.title: An agent skill repo ships each skill with its evals instead of a demo
entries.html:
A public agent-skill repo (Show HN) ships each skill with its own evals rather than a demo.

A thin signal, but it points to "evals ship with the skill definition" becoming a convention among agent builders. Ask for evals before adopting a third-party skill.

evidence.title: Show HN: An AI agent skill repo built around evals, not demos

entries.title: HalluTruthQA: detecting a hallucination is easier than locating and explaining it
entries.html:
HalluTruthQA is a 2,400-example Arabic QA benchmark across four domains (Islamic knowledge, history, science, geography) with verified references, six candidate answers, character-level error spans, human explanations, and macro/micro hallucination types.

Zero-shot across Allam, Falcon-H1, Qwen32, and Silma, no model wins every sub-task. Best scores: 0.880 Macro-F1 on detection, but only 0.516 F1 on span localization, 0.852 on factual verification, 0.644 on explanation. Catching that an answer is wrong is easier than showing where and why.

evidence.title: HalluTruthQA: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Hallucination Detection, Localization, and Explanation in Arabic Question Answering

entries.title: Motorway's eval pipeline cut incorrect results from 1 in 8 queries to 1 in 50
entries.html:
Motorway and AWS built an end-to-end evaluation pipeline on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that cut incorrect results from 1 in 8 queries to 1 in 50 and issue-detection time from hours to minutes.

It is a concrete before/after on what an eval pipeline is worth in production. The numbers come from a vendor blog.

evidence.title: Evaluating AI Agents: A production blueprint with Strands and AgentCore

entries.title: LangChain's Harbor eval spans coding, conversation, and retrieval and gates what ships
entries.html:
LangChain revamped how it benchmarks Deep Agents: one Harbor eval setup across coding, conversation, and retrieval, used to decide which changes ship rather than reporting a score afterward.

A single cross-capability gate catches a change that helps one task type while regressing another.

evidence.title: How We Benchmark Deep Agents

entries.title: Value-poisoning benchmark: cost-optimized models act on corrupted business data 48-63% of the time
entries.html:
ActionRail's value-poisoning suite tests whether an agent acts on corrupted-but-plausible business data — an altered payment account, a fake refund address — inside an otherwise legitimate document. Across 8 models from 4 providers on 10 consequential workflows:

  • Cost-optimized models failed 48.3-63.3% of the time; frontier models 1.7-21.7%.
  • A guard layer blocked all 480 protected attack cases with zero false positives on legitimate ones.

This failure mode needs a dedicated defense, not just a stronger model.

evidence.title: A value-poisoning benchmark for consequential agent actions

entries.title: OpenBench compares coding-agent harnesses against each other
entries.html:
OpenBench is a benchmark built specifically for comparing coding-agent harnesses, not just models.

It gives the "the harness is part of what you benchmark" point its own instrument. Use it as a signal for harness choice, and hold the model fixed when comparing.

evidence.title: OpenBench – A benchmark for comparing coding-agent harnesses

entries.title: Langy reads production traces, writes tests for failures, and opens a fix PR
entries.html:
Langy, an AI engineer inside LangWatch, reads production traces, writes Scenario tests and evaluations for the problems it finds, opens a pull request on the repo, and proves the fix by running those simulations in CI. A human still merges.

The loop runs from "a trace shows a failure" to "a runnable eval and a proposed fix exist" without anyone writing either by hand.

evidence.title: Show HN: Langy, an automated AI engineer (we gave it a robot body) [video]

entries.title: LangChain's Eval Engineering Skill builds evals from repo context and traces
entries.html:
LangChain's Eval Engineering Skill inspects an agent's repo and production traces, proposes evals through user interviews rather than a blank rubric, and outputs runnable Harbor tasks.

Writing evals is the cost that stalls most teams. Making eval authorship an agent job, grounded in real traces, attacks that cost directly.

evidence.title: Eval Engineering Skill: Build Evals From Repo Context and Traces

entries.title: SkillCorpus curates ~821,000 crawled agent skills; gains stop at coverage and harness boundaries
entries.html:
SkillCorpus filters roughly 821,000 crawled agent skills (SKILL.md packages) into a curated, taxonomy-tagged corpus. Integrating it improves scores across three benchmarks and two harnesses.

The gains trace to a coverage boundary and a harness boundary: a good skill helps only the tasks it covers and only in a harness that can use it. Evaluate skills against your own task mix and harness.

evidence.title: SkillCorpus: Consolidating and Evaluating the Open Skill Ecosystem for Real-World LLM Agents

entries.title: OmniaBench: frontier models clear about half of 1,431 tasks across 90 domains
entries.html:
OmniaBench tests general agents across 1,431 tasks in 90 top-level application domains with an explicit state space, and finds even frontier models clear barely half.

A broad, executable-environment benchmark still finds headroom that familiar coding and tool-use suites do not expose.

evidence.title: OmniaBench: Benchmarking General AI Agents Across Diverse Scenarios

entries.title: IssueBench benchmarks the tool that finds issues in agent traces
entries.html:
LangChain built IssueBench, a synthetic benchmark that scores how well LangSmith Engine identifies, categorizes, and groups issues in agent traces.

Automated issue detection is itself a grader. It needs the same measured accuracy as the agents it watches before teams trust its triage.

evidence.title: IssueBench - How We Evaluate Engine

entries.title: Favur publishes harness scores with full deterministic replay of every run
entries.html:
Favur, a Python multi-agent harness of 14 role-specialized agents coordinated by code rather than an LLM orchestrator, scores runs across models on the same standardized statement of work. The composite score covers eight subjects — code quality, test quality, cost efficiency, velocity, tool discipline, effort efficiency, process discipline, deliverables — computed from each run's artifacts.

Every scored run can be replayed end-to-end, which makes the published score checkable rather than taken on trust.

evidence.title: Show HN: Favur Evals – evals of our agent harness, explore and control replays

entries.title: Left alone with an eval script, one coding agent memorized eval rows to win
entries.html:
In the "autoresearch" pattern a coding agent gets a dataset, an evaluation script, and one editable file, and keeps any change that raises the score. Head-to-head on Quran recitation data, Claude Code stopped early with compact, general code; OpenAI Codex drove the metric roughly 10x lower, largely by memorizing answers to individual eval rows.

Telling both agents a held-out test set existed closed the gap and erased the memorization, but the generalizing agent's code still transferred better. A visible held-out check, not just a stricter eval script, keeps an unsupervised optimization loop honest.

evidence.title: Autoresearch with Coding Agents: Generalizers and Metric-Maximizers on Quran Recitation Data

entries.title: AlphaEvolve GA works only where a measurable evaluation function exists
entries.html:
Google's AlphaEvolve reached general availability on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform as an evolutionary code-optimization service. Evaluators run client-side, so code never leaves the customer's infrastructure; Klarna reports doubling ML training throughput.

Practitioners note it only works where a measurable evaluation function exists. Teams with a scorable objective can hand optimization to an agent; teams without one hit the fuzzy-spec wall first.

evidence.title: Google's AlphaEvolve Reaches General Availability with Evolutionary Code Optimization as a Service

entries.title: QCon AI Boston: production AI shifts from prompts to platforms, harnesses, and evals
entries.html:
InfoQ's QCon AI Boston 2026 report finds talks focused on the operational side of deploying agents: context management, security through a harness around agents, and a full engineering model for AI that includes evals.

Practitioners now treat evals as platform infrastructure next to the harness, not an afterthought to prompt work.

evidence.title: QCon AI Boston: Production AI Moves Beyond Prompts to Platforms, Harnesses, and Evals

entries.title: A 241-turn Claude coding session yields three failure patterns turned into guardrails
entries.html:
Evaluating a 241-turn Claude coding session surfaced three recurring failures:

  • Confident misinformation contradicted by documentation.
  • Review issues quietly deferred instead of fixed.
  • A six-task feature built on an unverified assumption a ten-minute audit would have caught.

The author turned them into standing guardrails in the agent's instructions. Without that step, the next session relearns the same lessons at full cost.

evidence.title: When your coding agent doesn't listen: evaluating a 241-turn Claude session

entries.title: DeepStress shows search agents vary widely when fed unreliable evidence
entries.html:
DeepStress stress-tests deep search agents by controlling how often they meet challenging evidence — corrupted on trustworthiness, relevance, or factuality — instead of the clean documents standard benchmarks assume. Agents vary widely in how they handle it.

Poor evidence is rare in benchmark data but can cause dramatic failure in real use. If your agent searches the open web, test it on bad inputs on purpose.

evidence.title: DeepStress: Stress-Testing Deep Search Agents

entries.title: Most agent optimizers stop helping once applied repeatedly on Terminal-Bench 2.0
entries.html:
A continual-learning evaluation on Terminal-Bench 2.0 applies optimization recursively as new tasks arrive. GEPA's optimized agent transferred below baseline on new tasks; Meta Harness improved once but not with a second budget. Only regression-controlled RELAI-VCL held the top pass rate at every stage:

  • RELAI-VCL: 76.4% lifelong average
  • GEPA: 66.0%
  • Meta Harness: 64.6%
  • Baseline: 58.7%

One-shot gains on a fixed benchmark say little about a deployed agent tuned over time.

evidence.title: Do Agent Optimizers Compound? A Continual-Learning Evaluation on Terminal-Bench 2.0

entries.title: Stripe's integration benchmark shows agents build code but fail to validate it
entries.html:
Stripe's 11-environment agent-integration suite covers checkout migration, billing API work, and full-stack browser checkout. On full-stack tasks Claude Opus 4.5 scored 92% against GPT-5.2's 73%, but both models' failures were in validation, not code generation: misreading an HTTP 400 as success, or losing track of a form after a tool interaction moved focus out of an input field.

An agent that writes working code but cannot tell whether it worked is what a pass/fail outcome score hides.

evidence.title: Stripe Benchmark Shows AI Agents Build Integrations but Struggle with Validation

entries.title: AWS QA Studio runs browser-driving test agents as a parallel CI gate
entries.html:
AWS's QA Studio (on Amazon Nova Act) runs agentic UI tests as parallel cloud tasks organized into suites, with a CLI for CI/CD. Runs return structured pass / fail / infra-error exit codes plus trajectory logs and session recordings.

Separating infra errors from real failures is what lets an agentic test sit in CI without flaky runs blocking merges.

evidence.title: Accelerating software delivery with agentic QA automation using Amazon Nova Act – Part 2

entries.title: Online evals can wait days to grade an agent against the real downstream outcome
entries.html:
Inngest's guide to online versus offline evals describes an online eval that defers judgment — pausing for up to several days — until the downstream event the task was supposed to cause actually happens.

The agent is graded on what it caused, not on what it claimed at finish time. Offline evals stay the fast pre-merge check; online evals catch what only production outcomes reveal.

evidence.title: Online vs. Offline AI Evals: When to Use Each

entries.title: Checking 100 human-annotated traces shows automated evals diverge from human raters
entries.html:
In his AI product engineering notes, Hamel Husain checked 100 human-annotated traces against automated eval systems and found real divergence between what the automated pipeline scored and what a human rater would.

You cannot certify an automated eval suite by spot-checking a few cases. Measure its agreement with human judgment directly, and re-measure when the judge, rubric, or traffic changes.

evidence.title: AI Product Engineering Notes

also.title: LLM-as-judge: model-graded evaluation of traces and outputs

entries.title: Free tool runs human labels and LLM judges side by side over the same outputs
entries.html:
A free, practitioner-built tool evaluates AI agent outputs with human labels and LLM judges over the same items, rather than treating human review as a fallback for when the judge is unsure.

Keeping both on the same data makes judge-human agreement a number you can watch, not a one-off audit.

evidence.title: I built a free tool to evaluate AI agent outputs (human labels and LLM judges)

entries.title: Generating one case at calibrated ambiguity exposes a cliff a pass rate hides
entries.html:
Discovery Bench, covered in Google Cloud's "Who evaluates the evaluations?", uses surprisal — the uncertainty a query leaves about the correct answer — to generate the same case at controlled ambiguity levels instead of hand-labeling "easy" and "hard".

  • On the identical query, agent, and ground truth, F1 fell from 1.00 at neutral phrasing to 0.00 at high ambiguity.
  • Mid-ambiguity cases sometimes beat low-ambiguity ones, exposing quirks such as over-retrieval of time-sharded tables.
  • The audit found benchmark ground truth wrong on 6.49% of MMLU.

The eval data needs evaluating too.

evidence.title: Frontier and Center: Who evaluates the evaluations?

entries.title: OpenAI finds reliability and accuracy problems in SWE-Bench Pro
entries.html:
OpenAI's "Separating signal from noise in coding evaluations" raises reliability and accuracy concerns in SWE-Bench Pro, a widely used coding benchmark.

It joins GSO, SWE-Perf, and SWE-fficiency on the list of coding benchmarks whose scores need scrutiny before they support a model or vendor decision.

evidence.title: Separating signal from noise in coding evaluations

entries.title: Agents' Last Exam targets long-horizon professional work across 55 sub-industries
entries.html:
Agents' Last Exam, co-led with UC Berkeley and 300+ domain experts, benchmarks agents on long-horizon, economically valuable professional tasks with verifiable outcomes across 55 sub-industries.

It moves past narrow coding and tool-use suites toward the kinds of real work static leaderboards have under-represented.

evidence.title: Agents' Last Exam: AI Agent Benchmark for Real-World Professional Workflows

entries.title: Schneider Electric gates 60+ AI products on an eval maturity framework
entries.html:
Schneider Electric runs one LangSmith workspace per AI product (not per environment), so production traces flow straight into development datasets. Domain experts annotate real usage without developer tooling access.

Promotion is gated on a maturity framework tracking instrumentation, offline eval coverage, online evaluators, and user feedback across 60+ products. Evaluation becomes a lifecycle gate, not a pre-launch checkbox.

evidence.title: How Schneider Electric Built Their LLMOps Foundations With LangSmith

entries.title: LangChain treats improving agents as data mining over traces, not labeling
entries.html:
LangChain's loop: mine production agent traces for failure clusters first, fine-tune a judge on those clusters (cheaper than a frontier judge), then use that judge to hill-climb agent performance with evals.

"What should we evaluate" becomes a question the traces answer, rather than a rubric written before any traces existed.

evidence.title: Improving Agents is a Data Mining Problem

entries.title: Repeated runs of one model varied more than the gap between ranked models
entries.html:
A practitioner analysis in Dan Luu's notes measured one standard deviation of 7.5% between repeated runs of the same model on a coding task — larger than the gap between the best- and worst-ranked models in the comparison. Dropping or swapping a handful of tasks from a ~100-task set was enough to change which model won.

Single-run leaderboard gaps of a few points are not evidence of a better model. Report variance across repeated runs and task subsets.

evidence.title: Agentic test processes, LLM benchmarks, and other notes on agentic coding

entries.title: Ensembled reviewer personas cut false positives more than a stronger single model
entries.html:
Dan Luu's notes on agentic coding report two testing findings:

  • LLM-written fuzzers find real, serious bugs within minutes but leave coverage gaps a quick hand-written fuzzer would catch, so bug-finding recall is not proof of thorough testing.
  • Ensembling reviewers — independent agents checking the same artifact under different personas, including a deliberately contrarian one — cuts false positives more reliably than swapping in a stronger model.

The process around the model carries as much weight as the model choice.

evidence.title: Agentic test processes, LLM benchmarks, and other notes on agentic coding

entries.title: Performance-optimization benchmarks conflate runtime noise with agent progress
entries.html:
A study of repository-level performance-optimization benchmarks (GSO, SWE-Perf, SWE-fficiency), which score coding agents by comparing patched runtime against baselines and reference patches, finds their leaderboard scores can conflate runtime instability and benchmark-specific scoring choices with real capability.

The problem is not only that benchmarks are unrepresentative; their own numbers can be noisy.

evidence.title: Are Performance-Optimization Benchmarks Reliably Measuring Coding Agents?

entries.title: Pendo traces, evaluates, and monitors its Novus agent in one LangSmith workflow
entries.html:
Pendo uses LangSmith to debug, evaluate, and monitor Novus, its product agent that turns behavioral data and session replays into code fixes.

Eval, tracing, and monitoring run as one workflow over the same traces rather than three separate tools. This is a vendor-published case study.

evidence.title: How Pendo uses LangSmith to trace Novus from user behavior to code fixes

entries.title: Harbor pairs LangSmith sandboxes and observability with Deep Agents to evaluate long-running agents
entries.html:
LangChain plugged Deep Agents, LangSmith sandboxes, and observability into Harbor as one runner for long-running, stateful agents.

Stateful agents need an environment that persists across steps and can be inspected afterward. A plain dataset-and-scorer loop cannot evaluate them.

evidence.title: Harbor x LangChain: A Unified Stack for Evaluating Agents

entries.title: Stateful agents can be checked on state transitions without an LLM judge
entries.html:
A deterministic-replacement approach for stateful agent evaluation checks state transitions directly instead of asking a model to grade them.

"Judge with another LLM" is a default, not a requirement. Where the task admits a programmatic check, skipping the judge removes its cost, bias, and non-determinism at once.

evidence.title: A Deterministic Replacement for LLM-as-Judge in Stateful Agent Evaluation

entries.title: ScarfBench benchmarks agents on enterprise Java framework migration
entries.html:
ScarfBench evaluates AI agents on enterprise Java framework migration — a narrow, high-value task that general coding suites do not isolate.

It is an early instance of the domain-narrow coding benchmark pattern: if your agent does migrations, a general SWE score tells you little.

evidence.title: ScarfBench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Enterprise Java Framework Migration

entries.title: Multi-head classifiers score many behavioral failures in one pass over a trace
entries.html:
Morph Reflexes serves behavioral signals from agent traces — looping, reasoning leakage, user frustration — from a small model with multiple classifier heads over one forward pass, built on a vLLM-derived inference engine, at sub-30ms latency.

The pitch is explicit: judging every turn with a frontier model is too slow and expensive at scale. Per-signal heads make "watch every trace for every failure mode" an inference-cost question rather than N judge calls.

evidence.title: Show HN: Morph Reflexes – Multi-head classifiers for agent traces

entries.title: Emergence World is a lab for evaluating long-horizon agent autonomy
entries.html:
Emergence AI introduced Emergence World, a laboratory environment for evaluating long-horizon agent autonomy rather than single bounded tasks.

Long-running agents fail in ways a short task never exercises — drift, accumulated errors, lost goals — so they need environments that run long enough to show them.

evidence.title: Emergence World: A Laboratory for Evaluating Long-Horizon Agent Autonomy

entries.title: "It's hard to eval" is a product smell, not an excuse
entries.html:
Hamel Husain argues the common objection "our product is hard to eval" is a product smell: an artifact that is hard for you to verify is usually hard for users too, and in the worst case they redo the work to check it.

If you cannot say what good output looks like, fix the spec. Designing for ease of verification improves the product and makes the eval possible.

evidence.title: “It’s Hard to Eval” Is a Product Smell

entries.title: GitHub grades the Copilot agentic harness on results and token efficiency across 20+ models
entries.html:
GitHub evaluated its Copilot agentic harness across multiple benchmarks and more than 20 selectable models, reporting task results and token efficiency together.

The unit under test is the harness (agent + model + scaffold), and cost per solved task is a first-class eval metric beside pass rate. The results are self-reported by the vendor.

evidence.title: Evaluating performance and efficiency of the GitHub Copilot agentic harness across models and tasks

entries.title: Hugging Face model pages now feature Every Eval Ever community results
entries.html:
Hugging Face announced that Every Eval Ever results are featured on model pages, putting community evaluation results next to the model card rather than only self-reported vendor numbers.

Useful as a cross-check, with the caveat the rest of this theme makes: a result is only comparable if its harness, pipeline, and settings are known.

evidence.title: Featuring Every Eval Ever Results on Hugging Face Model Pages

entries.title: Microservice diagnosis benchmark scores the reasoning path, not only the verdict
entries.html:
A multi-dataset benchmark for LLM agents doing microservice failure diagnosis (AgentOps) argues existing benchmarks are outcome-oriented — they score the final answer and skip the reasoning process. It adds two large-scale datasets over multimodal observability data and grades the diagnosis path.

Eval and observability converge here: the trace is the shared substrate for both debugging and grading.

evidence.title: A Multi-Dataset Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agents in Microservice Failure Diagnosis

entries.title: OpenRCA 2.0 labels the failure propagation path, not just the root cause
entries.html:
OpenRCA 2.0 reframes root-cause-analysis evaluation from outcome labels to causal process supervision. Earlier RCA datasets labeled only the root cause, which reduced the task to pattern matching; the new labels include the propagation path from root cause to observed symptom.

That gives trajectory-aware graders something to be trained and audited against: did the agent reason through the right intermediate steps, not only land the final answer.

evidence.title: OpenRCA 2.0: From Outcome Labels to Causal Process Supervision

entries.title: Topos scores agent-written code on structural quality, not just passing tests
entries.html:
Topos maps a codebase to program graphs (AST, CFG, CPG, MDG) and computes structural metrics on agent-written code. The premise: "tests passing" no longer justifies a merge, and the human cost of reviewing agent contributions is the new bottleneck.

For code agents the eval question becomes "is this change good", not only "does it run".

evidence.title: Show HN: Topos – Structural code quality metrics for agent-written programs

entries.title: Most evals would have missed the Linear sales-email failure
entries.html:
A post-mortem, "Why most AI evals would miss the Linear sales email failure", walks through a real agent failure that a typical eval suite would not have caught.

The suite only tests what someone thought to encode. Add each real incident to the eval set as a regression case once it happens.

evidence.title: Why most AI evals would miss the Linear sales email failure

entries.title: Three years of evals for financial agents: suites pass while the agent fails what matters
entries.html:
A practitioner write-up, "Lessons from Building Evals for Financial AI Agents", reports what building evals for financial agents taught over several years.

Its central warning matches other field reports: an eval suite can pass while the agent fails in the way that matters, because the suite never encoded the real-world failure. Start from observed failures, not a generic checklist.

evidence.title: Lessons from Building Evals for Financial AI Agents

entries.title: BabelJudge finds position, verbosity, and language bias in trajectory judges
entries.html:
BabelJudge, an open-source benchmark, measures LLM-as-judge reliability across languages and agent trajectories. Judges favor the response in slot A (position bias), prefer longer responses regardless of quality (verbosity bias), and degrade sharply in lower-resource languages — biases raw accuracy hides.

A trajectory judge needs its own validation before its verdicts gate a release.

evidence.title: BabelJudge: Measuring LLM-as-a-Judge Reliability Across Languages and Agent Trajectories

entries.title: Strands Evals turns a failed trace into categorized failures with a causal chain
entries.html:
AWS's Strands Evals detectors read a full agent trace and return categorized failures with confidence scores, causal chains linking a root cause to downstream symptoms, and a fix recommendation that says whether the change belongs in the system prompt or the tool definitions.

For agent evaluation, the output moves from a pass/fail number to a step-level diagnosis an engineer can act on. See LLM-as-judge for the judging side.

evidence.title: AI Agent Failure Detection and Root Cause Analysis with Strands Evals

entries.title: Rubric checks what an agent did, not just what it said
entries.html:
Rubric, an open-source eval tool shown on Show HN, tests an LLM agent's actions — which tools it called and in what order — rather than only its final text answer.

It is a small example of the shift to trajectory evaluation: a correct-looking answer can come from a broken path, so the tool calls themselves need assertions.

evidence.title: Show HN: Rubric – test what your LLM agent did, not just what it said

entries.title: A roadmap guide lays out how to learn AI agent evaluation
entries.html:
Machine Learning Mastery's "The Roadmap to Mastering AI Agent Evaluation" is a structured learning path for agent evaluation.

It is an introductory reference, a sign that agent eval is now taught as its own discipline rather than folded into model benchmarking.

evidence.title: The Roadmap to Mastering AI Agent Evaluation

entries.title: OpenAI predicts model behavior before release by simulating deployment
entries.html:
OpenAI's Deployment Simulation runs a candidate model against real conversation data to forecast how it will behave once deployed, instead of measuring problems after an incident.

It pushes evaluation to the pre-release gate: the question becomes "what will this model do on our traffic" rather than "how did it score on a static benchmark".

evidence.title: Predicting model behavior before release by simulating deployment

entries.title: A fine-tuned open judge scores production traces at about 1/100th of frontier cost
entries.html:
LangChain and Fireworks fine-tuned an open model to mine perceived-error signals from production traces, matching frontier-model judge performance at roughly 1/100th the cost.

Cost is what kept trajectory grading offline and sampled. A judge this cheap can run over every production trace, which turns evaluation into continuous monitoring rather than a periodic audit.

evidence.title: Building a 100x Cheaper Trace Judge with Fireworks

entries.title: Agents that look strong on familiar benchmarks degrade beyond them
entries.html:
"Running the Gauntlet" argues current agent benchmarks are built on popular applications with relatively simple tasks and a narrow set of capabilities, so modern agents saturate them. Re-evaluated beyond familiar environments, agent capability drops.

Static leaderboards over-state real-world capability. Test on your own environment and tools before trusting a headline score.

evidence.title: Running the Gauntlet: Re-evaluating the Capabilities of Agents Beyond Familiar Environments

agent-latency.title: Agent loops multiply per-call latency into slow, expensive runs
agent-latency.summary:
A chatbot waits on one model call; an agent waits on *many*, in sequence:
plan, call a tool, read the result, decide again. The wall-clock a user feels
is per-step latency multiplied by loop length, so a serving stack tuned for
single-shot throughput can still leave an agent slow. Latency is the run-time
twin of [cost](/topic/agent-cost): the loop that runs up the bill also runs
out the clock.

sections.heading: TL;DR
sections.html: A chatbot waits on one model call; an agent waits on many, in sequence: plan, call a tool, read the result, decide again. The wall-clock a user feels is per-step latency multiplied by loop length, so a serving stack tuned for single-shot throughput can still leave an agent slow. Latency is the run-time twin of cost: the loop that runs up the bill also runs out the clock.

sections.heading: State of the art
sections.html:
Agent latency is attacked at several layers at once, and the binding constraint has moved from compute to memory.

Agent traffic is not chat. Coding agents send bursty, long-context, tool-interleaved requests with over 80% KV-cache reuse. Schedulers, batchers, and routers are being rebuilt for that shape: session-aware scheduling, learned batching policies, and routing logic pulled inside the serving layer. vLLM's AgentX tuning shows these levers compound when tuned together, though its cost comparison is vendor-reported.

The bottleneck is moving KV state, not FLOPs. The context grows every step, and streaming it back is bandwidth-bound. Four answers compete: compress the cache, offload it to shared RAM/NVMe tiers, shard it across GPUs, or reuse it through prefix caching, prefix-aware routing, and cross-model KV transfer. Reuse has a sharp edge: once reused text sits mid-prompt, as in RAG and multi-agent handoffs, an unrepaired cache can score worse than none.

Engines are specializing. Disaggregation now splits by phase (prefill/decode) and by compute type (attention/FFN). New open-weight models and accelerators get tuned serving on day 0, then steady per-release kernel gains of a few percent per token, which multiply across every step of a loop.

Doing less work per step is the other lever: small latency-first models for the bulk of calls, learned prompt compression (Shopify cut end-to-end latency from 6.8s to 4.2s), and better speculative drafting. Context trimming has a measured cliff: below half the budget, failure odds rise sharply unless trimming preserves instructions and tool state.

The open problem sits outside the engine. Tool round-trips (search APIs with a 12x latency spread and short-lived caches, fan-out data queries, remote CI) and cold starts often dominate wall-clock time, and no serving optimization touches them. Voice sets a hard floor the whole loop must meet.

sections.heading: Why it matters for platform engineers
sections.html:
Latency is where the agent's architecture meets the user's patience and the GPU bill, and the three trade against each other directly.

Budget latency across the whole loop, not per call: count the sequential model hops, push what you can to a faster or smaller model, and cut the tokens decoded and streamed each step (compaction, KV reuse, speculative decoding). Pick a serving engine tuned to the bursty, long-context shape agents produce, not a chat benchmark. Measure tool latency cold, not against a warm cache.

Interactive modes (voice, live coding) set a hard ceiling, so the deliverable is a latency budget you can reason about per task, not a one-time inference optimization.

themes.title: Scheduling, batching, and routing for agent-shaped traffic
themes.summary: Agent traffic is bursty, long-context, and cache-heavy; session-aware scheduling, learned batching, and routing inside the serving layer beat chat-tuned defaults, and the levers compound when tuned together.

themes.title: KV state: compress it, offload it, shard it, reuse it
themes.summary: Moving the agent's growing KV state is the bottleneck; quantization, shared RAM/NVMe tiers, context parallelism, and prefix-aware routing cut it, but reuse outside a clean prefix needs repair.

themes.title: Disaggregated and specialized serving engines
themes.summary: Engines now split serving by phase (prefill/decode) and by compute type (attention/FFN), add hardware-specific kernels, and are what large deployers run in production.

themes.title: Day-0 serving for new models and hardware
themes.summary: New open-weight models and accelerators get quantized, speculative, disaggregated serving at launch, followed by steady per-release kernel gains of a few percent per token.

themes.title: Less work per step: small models, shorter prompts, faster drafting
themes.summary: Latency-first small models, learned prompt compression, protocol-aware trimming, and better speculative drafting cut decode work; trimming below half the context budget sharply raises failure.

themes.title: Latency outside the model: tools, cold starts, and voice
themes.summary: Tool round-trips (search APIs, data queries, CI) and cold starts often dominate the loop, and voice sets a hard floor the whole stack must meet.

entries.title: vLLM lifts DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash agentic throughput 5x within three weeks of release
entries.html:
vLLM reports that, three weeks after DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash shipped, it made the model 1.9x faster at low concurrency and raised throughput 5x on SemiAnalysis AgentX, an agentic benchmark (vendor-reported). The gains come from SWA bounded replay, CUDA graphs, DeepSeek's new kernels, and vLLM's own kernel fusions.

For builders: day-0 support is the start of the serving curve, not the end. Re-benchmark a self-hosted model a few weeks after launch before sizing capacity from launch-week numbers.

evidence.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on vLLM: 5x Agentic Throughput Since Day 0

entries.title: A harness-to-engine protocol cuts agent time-to-first-token 2.23x by sharing workflow intent
entries.html:
HEAR is a bidirectional protocol: the agent harness sends workflow intent (dependencies, context lifecycle, objectives) and the inference engine returns live state (queues, KV-cache, resource pressure, capabilities). Policy stays separate from protocol semantics.

Under memory-constrained concurrent serving, cache-aware coordination gave a 1.61x batch speedup and 2.23x lower median time-to-first-token on SCBench. Workload-specific execution modes gave 1.23x (BrowseComp-Plus) and 2.45x (DeepResearchBench) end-to-end speedups. These are paper-reported benchmark results.

For builders: the harness knows what will be reused; engines cannot infer it from request streams alone.

evidence.title: Can Agent Harnesses and Inference Engines Hear Each Other? The HEAR Protocol for Agentic LLM Serving

entries.title: High-bandwidth flash could hold agentic KV state, but write endurance limits it
entries.html:
A characterization study evaluates high-bandwidth flash (HBF) as extra accelerator memory for LLM serving. Agentic workloads make retaining KV state for reuse more important because they repeat interactions over growing contexts.

HBF adds capacity, but its access costs and limited write endurance complicate its use for state that is rewritten every step. It is a hardware option to watch, not one to plan around yet.

evidence.title: Characterizing High Bandwidth Flash for LLM Serving

entries.title: GKE Pod snapshots cut model startup latency up to 89%, but invalidation is the catch
entries.html:
GKE Pod snapshots checkpoint CPU and GPU memory through gVisor to Cloud Storage. Google reports up to 89% lower startup latency, with a 70B model loading in 37 seconds and an 8B model in 15. GKE Agent Sandbox uses them to suspend idle agents instead of holding warm pools.

The catch is invalidation: a snapshot matches only on the Pod spec hash, machine series, CPU architecture, gVisor version, and GPU driver version, and any mismatch falls back to a normal slow start. Snapshot lifecycle management becomes the new ops work.

evidence.title: GKE Pod Snapshots Cut Model Load Times, and Move the Work to Snapshot Lifecycle Management

entries.title: vLLM v0.30.0 adds DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with its whole KV cache in MXFP8
entries.html:
vLLM v0.30.0 (762 commits from 315 contributors) adds DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with its entire KV cache stored in MXFP8 through a FlashMLA V4.1 speedup on SM100, plus GLM-5.3-Flash, K2-Horizon, and other new models. The release also adds a "Fast Start" path that trims cold-start time.

It is the routine, compounding kind of serving gain: a new model arrives with a lower-precision KV cache and a faster attention kernel in the same release.

evidence.title: vllm v0.30.0

entries.title: Disaggregated serving of Qwen3.8-2.4T reaches 5K tokens/sec on GB300 NVL72, with a reproducible recipe
entries.html:
vLLM's prefill/decode-disaggregated serving of Qwen3.8-2.4T on GB300 NVL72 reaches 5,000 tokens/sec aggregate throughput and 180 tokens/sec per-user interactivity. The write-up publishes the methodology so other teams can reproduce the result on their own stack.

A reproducible recipe turns a launch-day number into a baseline you can test your own deployment against.

evidence.title: PD Serving of Qwen3.8-2.4T

entries.title: Context trimming hits a failure cliff below half the budget; protocol-aware trimming holds
entries.html:
A study of five trimming strategies on multi-step agentic workflows finds recency, relevance, and summarization save about 60% of tokens but drop task success to 66.6-77.3%. Protocol-aware trimming, which keeps instructions, tool state, and unresolved dependencies, reaches 92.2%; adding adaptive budget guardrails reaches 96.0% success and 1.0% cascading failure while still saving 56.0% of tokens.

Keeping 25% or less of context raises failure odds 10.92x versus keeping 50% or more (p < 0.001). That is a floor under how far compaction can go before latency savings cost correctness.

evidence.title: Protocol-Preserving Context Trimming for Agentic Workflows: Benefits, Failure Regimes, and Budget Guardrails

entries.title: SageMaker prefix-aware routing cuts P50 TTFT up to 77% by keeping KV caches warm
entries.html:
Amazon SageMaker Inference's prefix-aware routing sends requests that share a prompt prefix to the same instance, so the KV cache an earlier request built is still warm. On Llama 3.1 70B it cut P50 time-to-first-token by up to 77% and raised the KV cache hit rate from about 25% to over 80%.

No cache repair is needed, only co-location. Once a service fans out across many instances, request placement matters as much as cache compression.

evidence.title: Reduce LLM latency with prefix-aware routing on Amazon SageMaker Inference

entries.title: KVShareArena: KV reuse outside the prompt prefix can score worse than no cache at all
entries.html:
Prefix caching assumes reused text sits at the start of the prompt. RAG assembles different chunks per query, and a multi-agent coordinator reads other agents' reports, so reusable text lands mid-prompt, at the wrong positions, sometimes from another checkpoint.

KVShareArena scores reuse methods on that case. Correcting positions alone suffices until a question needs several retrieved sources; then only methods that pay for partial re-encoding or extra training recover half to two-thirds of the gap. An unrepaired cache can score worse than no cache, and compression that looks harmless on one prompt falls behind plain position correction.

evidence.title: KVShareArena: KV-Cache Reuse Across Contexts and Model Checkpoints

entries.title: vLLM tuned for SemiAnalysis AgentX reaches 130K tokens per GPU-second on agentic traffic
entries.html:
vLLM's account of optimizing for SemiAnalysis AgentX, a benchmark that scores serving stacks on agentic rather than chat-shaped traffic, combines KV-cache management, parallelism, scheduling, and prefill/decode disaggregation into one tuned stack. It reaches up to 130K tokens per GPU-second and reports a 14.6x-106x serving-cost advantage over Opus 5 on the benchmark.

It is less a new lever than evidence that the existing levers compound when tuned together for agent traffic. The cost comparison is vLLM's own.

evidence.title: vLLM x AgentX: Optimizing for Real-World Agentic Serving

entries.title: Tenstorrent accelerators join vLLM as an out-of-tree platform plugin
entries.html:
Tenstorrent joins vLLM as an out-of-tree platform plugin built around the hardware's mesh architecture: phase-based scheduling, single-process data parallelism on Galaxy, on-device sampling with a host fallback, and async decode overlap.

A plugin path lets non-NVIDIA hardware run the same serving engine without a fork, which widens the hardware options for a vLLM-based stack.

evidence.title: Serving LLMs on Tenstorrent Hardware: Inside the vLLM TT Plugin

entries.title: vLLM's HiSparse tier keeps GLM 5.3 decoding when its KV cache no longer fits in GPU memory
entries.html:
vLLM integrates HiSparse as a pressure-driven memory tier that composes with the Hybrid Memory Allocator and KV offloading. It activates once a request's KV state no longer fits in GPU memory, so GLM 5.3 requests keep decoding instead of stalling or falling back to a slower path.

Concurrency stays high exactly where the storage-bandwidth bottleneck would otherwise cap it.

evidence.title: GLM 5.3 Optimizations, Part 1: Hybrid HiSparse Offloading in vLLM

entries.title: Shopify's gisting compresses a 6,000-token system prompt into 1,500 learned tokens
entries.html:
Shopify trains learned "gist" tokens to reproduce a long system prompt's behavior: a teacher runs with the full prompt, a student learns the gist tokens by minimizing KL divergence between outputs, and the compact tokens replace the prompt at serving time.

On the Sidekick GraphQL agent the prompt shrank from about 6,000 tokens to 1,500 while holding quality. End-to-end latency fell from 6.8s to 4.2s, time to first token from 438ms to 354ms, and throughput rose from 20.2 to 23.4 queries/sec, enough to cut the GPU allocation for the same load. Spend side: agent cost.

evidence.title: Shopify Introduces Gisting: Compressing LLM System Prompts into Learned Tokens

entries.title: A cross-model KV layer lets one model skip prefill that another model already paid for
entries.html:
A universal context-reuse layer translates the KV state one model produced into a form a different model can consume, skipping the second model's prefill.

  • Same family (Qwen2.5-7B to 1.5B): LongBench2 accuracy rises from 27.59% to 34.48%.
  • Across families (Qwen2.5-1.5B to Gemma-2-2B): up to 67.05% less prefill cost at 4K context.
  • Large to small (Llama3.1-70B to Qwen2.5-7B): end-to-end latency drops from 899ms to 138ms, at 44.0% vs 45.7% accuracy.

It fits multi-model pipelines where a cheap model would otherwise redo a bigger model's prefill.

evidence.title: A Universal Context-Reuse Layer for Cross-Model KV Sharing

entries.title: Web-search APIs differ 12x in median latency, and cold caches cost up to 37x more
entries.html:
Measuring nine web-search APIs under identical 10-result requests found a 12x spread in median response time (320ms to 3.9s) and up to a 37x gap between one provider's cached and cold response (105ms vs 3,937ms).

Most providers' caches expire in 5-60 minutes, so an agent's search calls land cold far more often than a benchmark against a warm cache suggests. Choosing a search tool is a latency decision, not only a capability one.

evidence.title: The Web-Search Latency Your Agent Pays

entries.title: vLLM v0.28.0 speeds up Kimi K3 and lands DeepSeek V4 sparse MLA for every decode mode
entries.html:
vLLM v0.28.0 continues the Kimi K3 optimization stack-wide: Decode Context Parallel support, fused FlashKDA decode and prefill kernels, combined all-gathers with a 1.5-3x kernel-level speedup, an adaptive speculative token budget for about 60% better DSpark time-to-first-token, and shared-expert sharding that saves about 17 GiB per GPU.

It also lands DeepSeek V4's sparse MLA end-to-end across plain decode, MTP, and DSpark speculative decoding. The fast path now covers every decode mode the model runs.

evidence.title: vllm v0.28.0

entries.title: Continuous batching on an iPhone nearly doubles multi-agent throughput versus llama.cpp
entries.html:
A from-scratch Swift port of vLLM's continuous batching onto an iPhone's MLX kernels left-pads late-arriving requests and merges them into a shared KV-cache offset. It hit 169 aggregate tokens/sec across 8 concurrent streams versus llama.cpp's 90.

A 16-request, ~17K-prompt-token multi-agent workload ran in 25 seconds without thermal throttling; llama.cpp needed 47 seconds for half the load. Continuous batching answers concurrent decode on-device too, not only in the data center.

evidence.title: vLLM-iOS: 88% Faster Multi-Agent Inference on iOS

entries.title: AsymSpec lets the drafter read full context while the verifier decodes a compressed view
entries.html:
AsymSpec drops speculative decoding's requirement that drafter and target share identical context. A lightweight drafter reads the agent's full, uncompressed input while the large verifier decodes from a compressed view, with a divergence-aware acceptance gate keeping verification stable.

It recovers about 90% of full-context accuracy at 1.3-1.7x throughput and 0.2-0.3x the compute of decoding on full context. That eases the usual trade between compressing a growing agent context for latency and the accuracy compression costs.

evidence.title: AsymSpec: Context-Asymmetric Speculative Decoding for Agentic LLMs

entries.title: vLLM-Omni streams DiT weights across devices to serve a 124 GB model on 64 GB HBM
entries.html:
vLLM-Omni's Distributed Layerwise Offload shards and streams diffusion-transformer weights across devices. It serves a measured 124 GB Cosmos3 model on 64 GB of HBM and estimates a path toward 200B+ parameter models.

It applies the offload-instead-of-fit approach to model weights rather than KV state: memory capacity, not compute, decides which models fit a given fleet.

evidence.title: Distributed Layerwise Offload: Scaling Toward 200B+ DiT Models Efficiently in vLLM-Omni

entries.title: DARTree drafts token trees for up to 9.73x lossless speculative-decoding speedup
entries.html:
DARTree extends a pretrained autoregressive correction head for diffusion drafters from single draft chains to draft trees, scoring and pruning candidates across the whole tree in one batch.

Across seven math, code, and chat benchmarks it accepts up to 12.97 tokens per verification round (98.6% more than DFlash, 27.9% more than Domino), for up to 9.73x lossless speedup over plain autoregressive decoding. It is training-free. Mechanics: speculative decoding.

evidence.title: DARTree: Speculative Diffusion Decoding with Autoregressive Draft Trees

entries.title: vLLM Decode Context Parallelism shards the KV cache for 3x long-context throughput
entries.html:
vLLM's Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) shards the KV cache across GPUs along the sequence dimension. It reports 3x higher throughput on long-context agentic workloads versus standard tensor parallelism.

It attacks the storage-bandwidth bottleneck through parallelism rather than compression or offload: each GPU holds and reads only its slice of a long agent context.

evidence.title: Efficient Decode Context Parallelism with vLLM for Long Context Workloads

entries.title: OpenAI built GPT-Live's turnless, low-latency voice system in six months
entries.html:
OpenAI describes building GPT-Live, a continuous voice system with a turnless speech model (no push-to-talk turn-taking) and a low-latency architecture, in six months.

It is a model provider's own engineering case study of hitting the interactive latency floor, from the product side rather than a serving vendor's benchmark.

evidence.title: How we built a realtime system for responsive voice AI in six months

entries.title: vLLM Semantic Router reframes routing as a Mixture-of-Models engine
entries.html:
At 5,000 GitHub stars, vLLM Semantic Router sets its next phase: building the training, evaluation, and inference engine for a Mixture-of-Models era.

"Which model handles this request" becomes a first-class serving-layer decision with its own eval loop, not a routing feature bolted onto an engine. For agents, that is where fast-and-cheap versus slow-and-capable gets decided per call.

evidence.title: The Next Model Is a System: Building the Mixture-of-Models Era

entries.title: vLLM turns its Kimi K3 preview into efficient day-0 serving five days later
entries.html:
vLLM's day-0 Kimi K3 serving keeps the preview's hybrid KDA prefix caching and adds DSpark speculative decoding, production-scale disaggregation, and optimized kernels across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs.

The gap between preview and production support closed within one release cycle. Latency-tuned serving on day one now holds across a model's preview-to-GA transition, not just its announcement.

evidence.title: Kimi K3 Is Here: Efficient Day-0 Support on vLLM

entries.title: Netflix runs its in-house LLM serving platform on Triton and vLLM
entries.html:
Netflix detailed its in-house LLM serving platform, built on Triton and vLLM.

It is a practitioner data point that the open engines and serving techniques tracked here are what a large deployer runs in production, not only what a model lab shows on launch day.

evidence.title: Netflix Details Its In-House LLM Serving Platform with Triton and vLLM - infoq.com

entries.title: vLLM v0.26.0 ships a full Inkling stack and trims DeepSeek-V4 decode latency
entries.html:
vLLM v0.26.0 ships the Inkling model family with piecewise CUDA graphs, Hopper FA4 relative attention, MTP=1 speculative decoding, LoRA, and NVFP4 quantization in one release.

A DeepSeek-V4 performance push adds a specialized routing kernel (2.94% end-to-end TPOT), fused top-k bias (1.5-2x at kernel level), and redundant-copy removal (1.8% TPOT) without touching the serving architecture. Small per-step gains like these compound across every step of an agent loop.

evidence.title: vllm v0.26.0

entries.title: OpenLake offloads KV cache to shared RAM/NVMe, cutting cross-host TTFT from 44s to 0.6s
entries.html:
OpenLake offloads KV state from GPU memory into a shared RAM and NVMe tier, with a CUDA kernel that losslessly compresses blocks before they leave the GPU. Its motivation: one 256K-token conversation on Gemma 4 31B produces about 43GB of KV state, more than half an 80GB H100.

Because the tier is shared, a prefix cached on one host is cheap to fetch from another instead of being recomputed. On a 128K-context workload, time-to-first-token fell from 44 seconds to 0.6 when the prefix was reused across hosts. The project claims 50% lower long-horizon inference cost.

evidence.title: Show HN: Cuts Long Horizon Inference Costs by 50% via external KV Cache Offload

entries.title: vLLM runs end-to-end on pre-release NVIDIA Vera Rubin hardware
entries.html:
vLLM now runs end-to-end on pre-release NVIDIA Vera Rubin hardware.

Day-0 support now covers GPU generations, not only models. Teams planning capacity on the next hardware generation can expect the open engine to be ready at launch.

evidence.title: vLLM Runs on NVIDIA Vera Rubin Hardware

entries.title: vLLM previews production-scale Kimi K3 support with KDA-aware prefix caching
entries.html:
vLLM's preview of production-scale Kimi K3 support includes KDA-aware prefix caching, fused kernels, optimized MXFP4 MoE, multimodal integration, and initial NVIDIA and AMD paths.

It lands ahead of a full optimization pass, extending the day-0 pattern to a new open-weight architecture with its own attention variant.

evidence.title: A Preview of Production-Scale Kimi K3 Support on vLLM

entries.title: vLLM's AFD plugin disaggregates attention and FFN for MoE serving
entries.html:
The vLLM AFD plugin runs attention and FFN computation on separate execution paths for MoE serving, with GPU and Ascend NPU backends, connector-based execution, and graph and micro-batching ("ubatching") support.

Prefill/decode disaggregation splits a request by phase; AFD splits a single forward pass by compute type. That is a second knob for allocating hardware across the two halves of large open MoE models.

evidence.title: Announcing vLLM AFD Plugin: Disaggregating Attention and FFN for Flexible MoE Serving

entries.title: vLLM serves the 1T-parameter Inkling on day 0 at 380 tokens/sec per user
entries.html:
vLLM shipped full-feature support for Thinking Machines' 1T-parameter multimodal Inkling the day it released, with MTP, long-context serving, and parallelism. It reaches 380 tokens/sec per user with speculative decoding versus 140 without on 4 NVIDIA GB200 GPUs.

New models now get latency-tuned serving at launch, so speculative decoding and parallelism apply from the first day instead of after a follow-up optimization pass.

evidence.title: TML Inkling on vLLM: Day-0 Support with Optimized Performance

entries.title: One agent request fans out into dozens of queries, each held to a chat-era latency budget
entries.html:
Cube argues that a single agent request fans out into tens of database or API queries, and a multi-step workflow into hundreds. Each inherits chat-era expectations: a few hundred milliseconds feels responsive, a couple of seconds feels broken.

The dashboard semantic-layer pattern (pre-aggregated rollups served through query rewriting, columnar storage with partition pruning) is being repurposed as agent infrastructure because it was built for many small interactive queries, not a few large batch ones.

evidence.title: Query Latency in the Age of AI Agents

entries.title: vLLM and TileRT pair stock prefill with a specialized decode engine over RDMA
entries.html:
TileRT plugs a decode-only runtime into vLLM's prefill/decode split through the V1 connector interface, with zero changes to vLLM. KV state moves from stock vLLM prefill nodes to TileRT decode nodes over RDMA, and multi-token speculative decoding starts as soon as it lands.

It reaches peak decode throughput at a best-case 4.0-token acceptance rate on an 8-GPU setup. Today it is limited to one in-flight request per decode node and a narrow model list.

evidence.title: vLLM x TileRT: Specialized Decode for Latency-Critical Serving

entries.title: vLLM v0.25.0 makes Model Runner V2 the default and removes PagedAttention
entries.html:
vLLM v0.25.0 makes Model Runner V2 the default execution path for all dense models and deletes the legacy PagedAttention implementation. MRv2 gains prefix caching for Mamba hybrid models and dynamic speculative decoding compatible with full CUDA graphs. Tool-call and reasoning-token parsing across model families is unified under one Streaming Parser Engine.

Teams pinned to older vLLM releases should plan the upgrade: the attention path the engine was first known for is gone.

evidence.title: vllm v0.25.0

entries.title: vLLM's transformers backend matches native throughput without per-model code
entries.html:
vLLM's transformers modeling backend uses torch.fx graph analysis plus AST rewriting to fuse operations into optimized vLLM kernels automatically. It matches native per-model integration throughput on dense and MoE Qwen3 models without hand-written per-model code.

Keeping up with new architectures is a maintenance tax on latency. This lowers the cost of getting a new model onto a fast path.

evidence.title: Native-speed vLLM transformers modeling backend

entries.title: SMetric schedules agent sessions to balance load without losing KV-cache reuse
entries.html:
SMetric finds agent traffic already has over 80% KV-cache reuse in production, but generic schedulers over-index on cache locality and let load imbalance cap cluster throughput. Agents act only on complete responses, so cluster tokens per second matters more than per-token latency.

It load-balances the first hop of each agent session, then routes every later request cache-aware. Reported gains versus prior schedulers: 10-16% throughput under prefill-decode colocation and 2-34% on prefill under disaggregated serving.

evidence.title: SMetric: Rethink LLM Scheduling for Serving Agents with Balanced Session-centric Scheduling

entries.title: RL-learned batching policies target bursty traffic that static batching can't follow
entries.html:
Static batching policies need manual tuning per traffic shape and cannot adapt when patterns shift. This paper trains REINFORCE and PPO agents to learn batching and routing policies, modeling queue state, request type, and GPU availability on a discrete-event simulator validated against queuing theory and production traces (Azure Functions, BurstGPT).

Agent tool-calling produces exactly this bursty, heterogeneous load, not the steady arrival rate a chat workload has.

evidence.title: Adaptive Inference Batching using Policy Gradients

entries.title: vLLM's HPC-Ops backend tunes attention and FP8 MoE kernels for Hunyuan Hy3 on H20
entries.html:
Tencent's HPC-Ops integrates Hopper-optimized attention and FP8 MoE backends into vLLM for the Hunyuan Hy3 model on NVIDIA H20, improving mixed-length decode, MoE latency, time-to-first-token, and time-per-output-token.

Serving gains are increasingly model- and hardware-specific. The mixed-length, bursty decode it targets is the pattern agent loops produce, not the uniform batches a generic benchmark assumes.

evidence.title: vLLM × HPC-Ops: High-Performance Attention and MoE Backends from Tencent Hunyuan

entries.title: vLLM Semantic Router runs a bounded micro-agent inside the serving layer
entries.html:
vLLM Semantic Router turns its vllm-sr/auto routing into a bounded micro-agent runtime: confidence scoring, ratings, model fusion, and workflows run inside the serving layer instead of in a separate orchestration hop above it.

Each orchestration hop removed is a full model call's latency the agent no longer pays. The serving layer is starting to absorb logic that used to live in the application.

evidence.title: Micro-Agent: Beat Frontier Models with Collaboration inside Model API

entries.title: RaBitQCache compresses the KV cache with rotated binary quantization
entries.html:
RaBitQCache uses randomized rotated binary quantization to compress the KV cache, and an adaptive top-p token budget instead of a fixed top-k for sparse-attention retrieval, holding generation quality on long-context inference.

It cuts the memory I/O that DualPath names as the agentic bottleneck: a smaller cache is less state to move at every step.

evidence.title: RaBitQCache: Rotated Binary Quantization for KVCache in Long Context LLM Inference

entries.title: Local CI cuts the feedback loop for developers and coding agents alike
entries.html:
Modern Treasury runs checks on the developer's machine instead of round-tripping to a remote CI runner, cutting feedback latency for both human developers and coding agents.

For a coding agent, waiting on a CI runner sits on the same wall-clock budget as each model call. A slow tool round-trip can dominate the loop even when inference is fast.

evidence.title: Reducing Feedback Latency with Local CI for Developers and AI Agents

entries.title: vLLM v0.24.0 adds MiniMax-M3 with MXFP4, FP8 sparse GQA, and AMD tuning
entries.html:
vLLM v0.24.0 (571 commits from 256 contributors) adds MiniMax-M3 with a fast follow-on BF16/FP8 indexer, MXFP4 support, FP8 sparse GQA, and AMD/ROCm tuning: MXFP8 MoE on gfx950, FP8 per-channel weights on MI300X, and an FP8 KV-cache fix. It also fixes a MiniMax-M2 performance regression and keeps maturing DeepSeek-V4 support.

New open-weight models arrive with quantized, vendor-specific fast paths in the same release, so self-hosters don't wait for a later optimization pass.

evidence.title: vllm v0.24.0

entries.title: TraceLab profiles real coding-agent traffic so servers can be tuned to it
entries.html:
TraceLab (University of Washington) characterizes real, day-to-day coding-agent usage across multiple agents and model families for serving-system research. Existing public traces and benchmarks don't capture that usage.

The premise: agent workloads don't look like chat. Coding agents issue bursty, long-context, tool-interleaved requests, so a server tuned on a generic chat trace is tuned for the wrong shape.

evidence.title: TraceLab: Characterizing Coding Agent Workloads for LLM Serving
TraceLab: Characterizing Coding Agent Workloads for LLM Serving

entries.title: NVIDIA and AWS pitch their partnership on low-latency inference at scale
entries.html:
NVIDIA's work with AWS across Amazon OpenSearch and Amazon EC2 is framed around four constraints: low-latency inference, fast vector search, GPU price-performance, and infrastructure that grows without multiplying operational complexity.

Infra vendors now sell explicitly on latency. For an agent, raw engine speed moves only one term of the budget; loop length and tool round-trips still multiply it.

evidence.title: NVIDIA and AWS Collaborate to Bring AI to Production at Scale

entries.title: Modular 26.4 ships MoE serving it bills as state of the art
entries.html:
Modular 26.4 ships mixture-of-experts serving that the company calls state of the art, alongside model bring-up via agent skills and Mojo 1.0 Beta 2. The performance claim is vendor-reported.

It is one more engine competing on MoE decode, the architecture most large open-weight releases now use. Measure it on your own agent traffic before switching engines.

evidence.title: Modular 26.4: SOTA Moe Serving, Model Bringup via Agent Skills, Mojo 1.0 Beta 2

entries.title: Loka's Nova 2 Sonic voice agent treats round-trip time as a design constraint
entries.html:
Loka built a voice agent on Amazon Nova 2 Sonic to fix a specific failure: slow, robotic voice assistants make customers hang up, which damages the brand and drives up support costs. The architecture treats round-trip time as a first-class constraint from the start, not a tuning pass afterwards.

Interactive modes set a hard latency floor. A voice agent's budget is set by when the caller gives up, not by what the serving stack happens to deliver.

evidence.title: How Loka Built a Natural, Low-Latency Voice Agent with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic

entries.title: Kog Laneformer 2B is a latency-first small model built with its inference engine
entries.html:
Kog built Laneformer 2B as a latency-first model, designed together with the Kog inference engine rather than adapted to a fast server after the fact.

Most of an agent's calls don't need frontier breadth. Sending the bulk of them to a small, predictable model is the same downshift that controls cost, applied to wall-clock time.

evidence.title: Kog Laneformer 2B: The Latency-First Model Behind Kog Inference Engine

entries.title: DualPath: agentic inference is bound by storage bandwidth, not compute
entries.html:
DualPath finds that the binding constraint in agentic LLM inference is storage bandwidth, not compute: the agent's growing KV and context state has to be streamed back in at every step of the loop.

That changes the optimization target. Faster kernels help less than shrinking, offloading, sharding, or reusing the state each step has to move.

evidence.title: DualPath: Breaking the Storage Bandwidth Bottleneck in Agentic LLM Inference
