agent-memory.title: Agents forget across steps and sessions
agent-memory.summary:
An agent's working memory is its context window, which is finite and resets
between runs. On long-horizon tasks it forgets earlier steps, repeats work, and
loses the user's intent — so "agent memory" (what to persist, where, and how to
recall it) becomes a first-class architecture problem rather than a prompt tweak.

sections.heading: TL;DR
sections.html: An agent's working memory is its context window, which is finite and resets between runs. On long-horizon tasks it forgets earlier steps, repeats work, and loses the user's intent — so "agent memory" (what to persist, where, and how to recall it) becomes a first-class architecture problem rather than a prompt tweak.

sections.heading: State of the art
sections.html:
The field has converged on memory as a tiered system: the live context window, an episodic log of past interactions, and a durable store of facts, preferences, and procedures. That split now ships as real components, often on infrastructure teams already run (Elasticsearch, Postgres, Redis) and often exposed over MCP. Newer framing treats memory as a lifecycle: deciding what to write, scoping it, consolidating, and forgetting.

The hard questions moved to the write and recall paths. Similarity search misses facts that are logically relevant but worded differently, and append-only stores keep stale facts alive; one study found a memory without revocation scores below no memory at all. Instruction files like CLAUDE.md show the write-side version: they grow because deleting a rule is riskier than adding one.

Build vs. buy is splitting the market. Managed services sit beside a crowded wave of local-first, single-file stores. Several of the latter retrieve with BM25 plus vectors and no LLM in the loop, and report recall in the mid-90s on LongMemEval.

Integrity is the open problem. Memory admits poisoned facts, hidden injections, forged reasoning, and sycophantic recall, and benchmarks show that strong recall does not predict whether an agent uses memory well. Evaluation is maturing toward fixed Add/Search pipelines and cost-aware scoring.

The counterweight is brute force: 1M-token windows and recursive dispatch let some runs skip memory engineering (see context compaction). They don't carry anything across sessions.

sections.heading: Why it matters for platform engineers
sections.html: Memory is where agent cost, latency, and reliability collide: stuffing everything into context is simple but blows up token cost and latency and still forgets; an external store adds a retrieval hop and a freshness/consistency problem. The decision (compact vs. retrieve vs. both, build vs. buy) is an infrastructure decision with an ongoing operational tail — eviction policies, index maintenance, revocation, per-user isolation, and recall evaluation — not a one-time integration. The write path is also a security boundary: anything an agent stores becomes trusted context later.

themes.title: Tiered and lifecycle memory architectures
themes.summary: Working, episodic, and long-term tiers are settled practice, now shipped as products on existing infrastructure, with newer work treating memory as a lifecycle of writing, scoping, consolidating, and forgetting.

themes.title: Build vs. buy: managed services and developer-owned stores
themes.summary: Managed memory services compete with a crowded wave of local-first, single-file stores that often retrieve with BM25 plus vectors and no LLM in the loop.

themes.title: Sharing memory across agents, isolating it between users
themes.summary: One memory now serves many agents and tools, which raises write-conflict and organization questions and forces per-user scoping so context doesn't leak between callers.

themes.title: What to write, when to revoke, how to recall
themes.summary: Similarity recall misses logically relevant and stale-but-superseded facts, so the work is shifting to revocation, write-time curation, and recall that reasons over the store.

themes.title: Poisoned, hidden, and sycophantic memory
themes.summary: Persistent memory is a persistent attack surface; poisoned facts, concealed injections, forged reasoning, and sycophancy all pass through the write path.

themes.title: Benchmarks and leaderboards for memory
themes.summary: Memory evaluation is moving from factual recall to utilization, failure modes, and task completion, scored through fixed pipelines with cost on the axis.

entries.title: DAEDALUS bootstraps agent memory from self-generated tasks, with no oracle verifier
entries.html:
An explorer agent invents challenging-but-solvable tasks in a new environment and a solver attempts them. Each solver failure yields a heuristic, which is accepted into the memory bank only after the solver repeatedly succeeds with it in context.

On AppWorld, τ²-bench, and AutomationBench the authors report up to +15.9 points mean success and up to 2.2x pass^5 over a no-memory baseline, competitive with methods that need training tasks. Heuristics also transferred to other model families.

For builders: gating writes on repeated success is a cheap write-time curation rule that needs no human-written guidelines.

evidence.title: DAEDALUS: Bootstrapping Agent Memory from Self-Generated Tasks

entries.title: Google puts server-side agent memory inside hardware enclaves the provider can't read
entries.html:
Google added private, server-side memory to Private AI Compute. Memory runs inside hardware-enforced secure enclaves, unlockable only with device-held keys, so context persists between sessions without the provider being able to read it.

It answers "remember across sessions without leaking" at the infrastructure layer, a privacy-by-construction guarantee rather than application-level scoping.

evidence.title: Advancing Private AI Compute with secure, server-side memory

entries.title: Managed Deep Agents 0.8 scopes memory to the authenticated user and denies it in group channels
entries.html:
LangChain's Managed Deep Agents 0.8 adds a two-tier memory config, define_memory(agent=MemoryLayer(), user=MemoryLayer()). User memory mounts at /memories/user/, keys to the caller's identity, and is allowed in one-to-one Slack DMs but denied by default in group chats and HTTP channels.

It pairs that with per-user credentials (OAuth across 23 services), so both what an agent remembers and what it can touch follow the caller. One user's context can't leak into another's conversation through a shared deployment.

evidence.title: Managed Deep Agents delivers a better user experience for agents in production

entries.title: Captain Memo, Memanto, and an open-source team store pitch one memory for every coding agent
entries.html:
Three more grassroots launches landed within a week:

  • Captain Memo: one local package of memory, skills, and capabilities any coding agent can use
  • an open-source shared memory for teams of AI coding agents
  • Memanto.ai, another agent memory service

They target the same cross-agent, cross-session recall gap as Sibyl and Awareness Local. Captain Memo's twist is packaging skills alongside memory.

evidence.title: Captain Memo – one local memory, skills and capabilities for every coding agent
Show HN: Open-source shared memory for teams of AI coding agents
Show HN: Memanto.ai

entries.title: DolphinBench scores memory by task completion and maps accuracy against cost
entries.html:
DolphinBench evaluates memory through an agent's task completion on real-world, action-dependent recall, not conversational QA where the question itself signals which fact to fetch. It also maps the Pareto frontier of accuracy against cost and latency instead of naming one winner.

Benchmarks that reward accuracy alone let memory systems make unreasonable cost trade-offs. Read memory leaderboards with the cost axis attached.

evidence.title: DolphinBench: Mapping the Pareto Frontier of Agent Memory

entries.title: AutoViewMem self-configures several views of the same memory and picks one per query
entries.html:
AutoViewMem argues that fixed granularities and static schemas fail when preferences, events, constraints, and temporal updates share one mixed representation; the interference makes top-K retrieval noisy.

Instead of one index, it maintains several complementary projections of the stored history and chooses which view to query per request. Like CABLE, it locates recall failures in the query interface, not only in what is stored.

evidence.title: AutoViewMem: Self-Configuring Orthogonal Views for Conversational Long-Term Memory

entries.title: OpenAI's V7 packages a company's scattered files as institutional memory for agents
entries.html:
V7, built on GPT-5.6, turns a company's scattered files into context agents use to complete complex, source-linked work.

Enterprise knowledge as memory now ships as a standalone agent product, not only as an internal platform layer like LinkedIn's playbooks or Elastic's Atlas. That puts a buy option next to the build path.

evidence.title: How V7 gives AI agents institutional memory

entries.title: MACE organizes shared multi-agent memory into scored units and averages 81.11% on eight benchmarks
entries.html:
MACE (Memory-Agent Co-Evolution) turns a multi-agent system's collaboration traces into functional memory units: conditions, actions, and outputs linked by support, conflict, and repair relations. Within a memory budget it picks which units and formats (instructions vs. checklists) to hand each agent, and updates unit scores from task outcomes.

It averages 81.11% across eight benchmarks, beating ten baselines. How shared memory is organized and presented back to agents is a tunable variable, not just whether writes conflict.

evidence.title: MACE: Memory-Agent Co-Evolution with Adaptive Memory Graphs for Multi-Agent Systems

also.title: Coordinating multiple agents adds more failure than capability

entries.title: Evaluating long-term agent memory has to look beyond context-window size
entries.html:
"Beyond Context Windows: Evaluating Long-Term Memory for AI Agents" argues that long-term memory evaluation must look past context-window size.

It is the evaluation-side version of the debate over whether bigger windows replace durable memory (see context compaction): a model's window spec says little about what it remembers across sessions.

evidence.title: Beyond Context Windows: Evaluating Long-Term Memory for AI Agents

entries.title: LinkedIn serves procedural memory and code search to coding agents over MCP
entries.html:
LinkedIn's Contextual Agent Playbooks and Tools, built on MCP, serve procedural memory, code search, and runbooks directly to coding agents to work around their limits in large codebases. LinkedIn reports a 20% productivity boost with zero loss in reliability (self-reported).

The tiered model built as a codebase-scoped organizational context layer, with operational guardrails, rather than a reference diagram.

evidence.title: Presentation: Context Engineering at LinkedIn: How We Built an Organizational Context Layer for AI Agents with MCP

also.title: Model Context Protocol: a standard interface for agent tools

entries.title: An open Add/Search evaluation framework makes agent memory systems comparable
entries.html:
An open evaluation framework defines agent memory by two fixed primitives, Add (write) and Search (retrieve), so different systems can be compared without each team choosing its own answer model and evaluation pipeline.

It extends the Agent Memory Leaderboard's approach into reusable tooling. Fixing the boundary between memory system and evaluator is what makes vendor numbers comparable.

evidence.title: Show HN: An open Add/Search evaluation framework for agent memory

entries.title: Make0 builds plug-and-play memory so Codex and Claude Code share context
entries.html:
Make0 AI is a personal memory layer meant to give Codex and Claude Code common context. The pain point is concrete: after hitting one agent's usage limit, switching tools means starting from scratch.

The author's first attempt, a shared Markdown instruction file, kept growing until the common context passed 20k tokens. A shared file without curation hits the same unbounded-growth problem as CLAUDE.md.

evidence.title: Working on Plug and Play personal AI Memory that works across AI agents

entries.title: LangChain's GTM agent learns per-rep style by diffing human edits against its drafts
entries.html:
LangChain's GTM Agent diffs a sales rep's edited draft against the agent's original to extract structured per-rep style observations. It writes them to Postgres keyed by rep and loads that record before every future draft, with a weekly cron job compacting the store. LangChain reports a 250% lift in lead conversion and 40 hours saved per rep per month.

The write is triggered by a human correcting the agent's output, a third write discipline beside automatic capture and explicit saves.

evidence.title: How we built LangChain’s GTM Agent

entries.title: SOS serves an explicitly saved project state to new coding-agent sessions over MCP
entries.html:
SOS stores a clearly defined "latest state" of a project inside the repository and serves it to a new or resumed session over MCP. The author built it because Codex kept losing track of what was done, which decisions still held, and what needed re-verification.

State is explicitly saved, not inferred. A superseded result stays in history but stops influencing the agent, the same guarantee TEPA's revocation targets, applied to project status.

evidence.title: Show HN: SOS – Project state between coding agent sessions

entries.title: COBRA-Skills cuts skill-optimization cost 55-58% with bandit-guided evaluation
entries.html:
COBRA-Skills frames skill improvement as budgeted sequential optimization over an evolving candidate pool. Contextual-bandit prioritization steers expensive execution-based evaluation toward the most promising or informative candidates instead of scoring every one.

Across six benchmarks and three target models it holds top-tier performance while cutting optimization cost 55-58% versus a SkillOpt baseline, with only 50 examples per benchmark. It makes the skill-evolution loop cheap enough to run routinely.

evidence.title: COBRA-Skills: Contextual Bandit-Guided Evolution for Agent Skill Optimization

entries.title: Fraise caps recall with a two-verb query language because the caller pays per token
entries.html:
Fraise is a single-binary memory database that stores facts as a temporal graph of facts, topics, and entities. It has exactly two verbs, remember and recall, for example recall billing entity:acme since:30d top:5.

Recall is ranked and capped, not exhaustive, with recent facts outranking older ones, on the stated reasoning that the caller pays for every token read back. Cost-consciousness moves from the storage format into the query interface.

evidence.title: Show HN: Fraise: a memory database for AI agents

entries.title: OKF Agent Memory stores git-tracked Markdown to Google's Open Knowledge Format spec
entries.html:
OKF Agent Memory keeps facts, decisions, and domain concepts as git-tracked Markdown with YAML front matter, implementing Google's Open Knowledge Format v0.2, which bakes in provenance, trust tiers, and lifecycle metadata.

Retrieval is in-memory BM25 with no vector database or embedding cost, returning in under 300 microseconds. A progressive-disclosure index lets the agent pull one concept at a time, cutting token use roughly 80% versus loading the whole knowledge base. It is the zero-LLM pattern built to a vendor-neutral spec.

evidence.title: OKF Agent Memory – Git-native persistent memory for AI coding agents

entries.title: A production context-engineering stack: Redis memory, summarization, reranking, semantic caching
entries.html:
Ricardo Ferreira's talk names the concrete stack behind the tiered-memory consensus:

  • Redis for both short-term and long-term memory
  • summarization to manage token limits
  • reranking and semantic caching to fight context rot
  • cost controls under strict latency constraints

It is the tiered split reduced to infrastructure a team would actually run.

evidence.title: Presentation: Beyond Prompting: Context Engineering for Production-Grade AI

entries.title: Hugging Face makes the case for coding-agent memory you own, not rent
entries.html:
Hugging Face's "Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own" (the Funes project) makes the "own your memory, don't rent it" pitch explicit.

A major platform endorsing developer-owned memory strengthens the local-first side of the build-vs-buy split against managed services like Cloudflare's Agent Memory.

evidence.title: Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

entries.title: MemHub adds persistent shared memory for AI coding agents
entries.html:
MemHub provides persistent, shared memory for AI coding agents.

It joins Sibyl and CMEM in targeting the same gap: several agents, or several sessions of one agent, working on the same codebase need to read one record of what has already been decided.

evidence.title: MemHub – Persistent shared memory for AI coding agents

entries.title: UTILMEM: strong recall scores don't predict whether an agent can use what it retrieved
entries.html:
UTILMEM (1,717 instances across five domains) scores memory utilization: reasoning over dense histories, catching implicitly relevant memories, synthesizing evidence across sessions, and resisting similar-looking distractors.

Strong scores on factual-recall benchmarks don't reliably predict utilization. Even when a system retrieves the right evidence, it often fails to integrate it or is misled by a plausible distractor. Retrieval alone is insufficient, and now it is separately measurable.

evidence.title: UTILMEM: Benchmarking Evidence Utilization in Long-Term Conversational Memory

also.title: An agent's answer is only as good as what it retrieved — and whether it can prove it

entries.title: Agent Zero Memory's citation lock lets answers cite only evidence actually retrieved
entries.html:
Agent Zero Memory splits a user's history into three parallel systems: an episodic timeline of what changed when, an entity-event knowledge graph, and a semantic store of durable facts. It enforces a citation lock: an answer may cite only evidence it actually retrieved, so the system abstains instead of guessing.

Provenance is built into the retrieval contract rather than checked after the fact, a structural defense against fabrication.

evidence.title: Agent Zero Memory: Provenance-Aware Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents

entries.title: Hours unattended: memory bugs compound in long, unsupervised coding-agent runs
entries.html:
A postmortem of an autonomous coding agent left running for hours unattended describes the memory bugs that broke it, which only surfaced once nobody was watching the session live.

Write-side curation failures compound in long, unsupervised runs. Memory needs monitoring the same way the agent's actions do.

evidence.title: Hours unattended: the memory bugs that broke my autonomous coding agent

entries.title: Contextual and OpenContext add project-local codebase memory for coding agents
entries.html:
Two more developer-owned stores shipped within days of each other:

  • Contextual: local codebase memory for AI coding agents
  • OpenContext: persistent, project-local memory served over MCP

Both keep memory inside the project rather than in a hosted service. The local-first roster is crowded enough that differentiation now comes from write discipline and recall quality, not from storing memory locally.

evidence.title: Show HN: Contextual – local codebase memory for AI coding agents
OpenContext – Persistent, project-local memory for AI coding agents via MCP

entries.title: Memctl adds git-style versioning and rollback to CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md
entries.html:
Memctl gives a coding agent's persistent instruction files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) versioning, diffing, and rollback.

It is a direct answer to catastrophic remembering: those files accumulate redundant, conflicting guidance, and without history there is no way to undo a bad edit.

evidence.title: Memctl: Versioned memory for your coding agent (Claude.md / AGENTS.md)

entries.title: Recuris evolves an agent's skill memory after each failure and improves 35 of 37 model-benchmark pairs
entries.html:
Recuris pairs a working memory that tracks task progress and guides skill selection with an experiential memory of reusable skills. After each failure, a meta-agent makes localized, validation-gated edits to the skill store.

It improves 35 of 37 model-benchmark pairs, gains reach +32.2 points on the longest-horizon tasks, and long-horizon failures drop by up to 80%. Skill memory pays off precisely where compaction and retrieval get harder.

evidence.title: Recursive Experiential-Working Memory Evolution for Long-Horizon Agent Harnesses

entries.title: Awareness Local hits 96.0% recall@5 on LongMemEval with no LLM in retrieval
entries.html:
Awareness Local stores memories as git-compatible Markdown, indexes them with SQLite FTS5 plus optional local embeddings, and retrieves with hybrid BM25-plus-vector reciprocal rank fusion, with no LLM in the loop. It reports 96.0% recall@5 on LongMemEval.

That is in the same range Sibyl reported on the same benchmark. Hybrid retrieval without an LLM is becoming a repeatable recipe, not one team's result.

evidence.title: Awareness Local: local-first memory for AI coding agents (96% R5 on LongMemEval)

entries.title: OpenWiki stores evidence-backed claims so codebase memory can correct itself
entries.html:
LangChain's self-correcting memory for OpenWiki stores evidence-backed claims instead of raw facts. It uses that evidence to detect when a claim has gone stale as the codebase changes, then corrects or drops it rather than retrieving whatever was written last.

It is a write-time defense against staleness and hallucination, pointed at codebase memory where the ground truth keeps moving.

evidence.title: Building Self-Correcting Memory in OpenWiki

entries.title: MemTrapBench: faithful, relevant memories can still distort an agent's reasoning
entries.html:
MemTrapBench targets memory-induced cognitive traps: even faithfully recorded, semantically relevant memories can distort reasoning or beliefs and degrade the current task.

Most memory benchmarks stop at whether information was extracted, stored, and retrieved correctly. Retaining information is necessary but not sufficient; how memory reshapes reasoning needs its own score.

evidence.title: MemTrapBench: Benchmarking Cognitive Traps in LLM Memory Use

entries.title: FTA-Mem anchors memory to fact, time, and affect for sparse long-term dialogue
entries.html:
FTA-Mem targets emotional-support agents, where dialogue is low-density: turns are incomplete, evidence is scattered, and user state shifts over time. Fixed units such as turn notes or session summaries either lose detail or add noise.

It segments conversations into coherent situation fragments and anchors memory to fact, time, and affect. For sparse, long relationships, the memory unit itself has to be designed, not just the store.

evidence.title: FTA-Mem: Fact-Time-Affect Anchored Memory for Low-Density Long-Term Dialogue

entries.title: CABLE: stored facts can still be unreachable through a bounded memory interface
entries.html:
CABLE names an evidence-reachability failure: even when a fact was stored correctly, later steps may not recover it through a bounded memory interface. Similarity retrieval handles topical recall but misses earlier plans or motivations that are semantically distant from the events they explain.

It adds antecedent-based links and expansion to reach that evidence. The interface, not just the store, limits what an agent can remember.

evidence.title: CABLE: Extending the Reach of Memory Retrieval via Complementary Antecedent-Based Linking and Expansion

also.title: An agent's answer is only as good as what it retrieved — and whether it can prove it

entries.title: How much memory does an agent need? Sizing as its own design question
entries.html:
A Hugging Face post on IBM Research's ALTK work asks how much memory an agent actually needs, treating memory sizing as a hierarchical-memory-management design question.

It is distinct from where memory lives or how stale facts get revoked. Sizing memory to the task is a cost decision a platform team makes before choosing a store.

evidence.title: How Much Memory Does Your Agent Actually Need?

entries.title: Agent Memory Leaderboard publishes first text-memory results across 69 frameworks
entries.html:
The Agent Memory Leaderboard released first results for text memory in two tracks, open-source methods and commercial products. 136 teams registered and 69 frameworks completed the run. Commercial leaders: MemoraX 58.02, MemOS 45.89, NTES-MEMORY-SMART 44.21.

Every entrant runs through one pipeline: memory system Add → Search, then benchmark Answer → Eval. A system can't win by picking its own answer model or evaluation setup, as vendor demos can.

evidence.title: Show HN: Agent Memory Leaderboard – first public results for AI memory systems

entries.title: MERIT keeps verified repairs as memory so later episodes don't rediscover the fix
entries.html:
Agents that repair a failure usually discard the successful correction, so a later episode with the same bug starts from scratch. MERIT, a training-free Text-to-SQL agent, keeps a dual-polarity memory of oracle-verified corrections and of directions that failed. A deterministic classifier assigns a coarse failure type that conditions retrieval, and only finalized earlier episodes are eligible.

"What worked last time, and why" becomes its own memory object, distinct from facts or preferences.

evidence.title: Causal Episodic Memory for Feedback-Driven Agent Repair

entries.title: CLAUDE.md keeps growing because deleting an instruction is costlier than adding one
entries.html:
Across 247,694 instruction lifetimes, agentic-coding files like CLAUDE.md grow without bound until the repo retires or someone rewrites the file. Appending is cheap; once an instruction's rationale is gone, deleting it safely costs O(2^|D|) for |D| instructions. The paper calls this catastrophic remembering, the inverse of catastrophic forgetting.

This store has no retrieval step: the whole file loads every turn. The fix is write-time deduplication and pruning, not better recall.

evidence.title: Why Does CLAUDE.md Keep Growing? Catastrophic Remembering in Agentic Coding

entries.title: Without revocation, stale memories make an agent worse than having no memory (TEPA)
entries.html:
TEPA represents each memory as a keyed precedent and revokes the active one the moment fresher evidence contradicts the same key, so old and new facts never coexist in the retrieval set.

Under full reversal, append-only and last-write-wins caches both score below no memory at all (0.210 vs. 0.309), while TEPA holds 0.950. A memory layer without revocation is not neutral on stale facts; it actively hurts.

evidence.title: TEPA: Revoking Stale Memories for Conflict-Robust Language Agents

entries.title: Remembrane makes agent recall deterministic enough to unit-test in CI
entries.html:
Remembrane keeps agent memory in one SQLite file with zero dependencies in the default install. Its author built it because a few thousand short strings didn't justify a hosted API, a vector database, or a framework.

The distinctive part: recall is deterministic, so you can write unit tests that assert what the agent remembers and run them in CI. Memory becomes something you can regression-test, not just observe.

evidence.title: Show HN: Remembrane – agent memory in one SQLite file, zero dependencies

entries.title: OpenLore bundles deterministic local memory with guardrails for coding agents
entries.html:
OpenLore packages deterministic, local-first memory together with guardrails for AI coding agents.

Shipping memory and guardrails in one package treats what an agent remembers and what it is allowed to do as one local control layer rather than two products.

evidence.title: OpenLore: Deterministic, local-first memory and guardrails for AI coding agents

entries.title: CMEM shares one local memory across Cursor, Claude Code, and CLI agents with sub-second recall
entries.html:
CMEM pairs a local SQLite store of timestamped observations (decisions, dead ends, fixes, not just diffs) with a built-in vector index. One MCP server exposes it to every client, so Cursor, Claude Code, and a bare CLI agent share the same memory, with recall reported under one second.

It bundles 11 skills so teams don't write the write/recall logic themselves (the vendor cites 6+ weeks for a custom build). It is Apache-2.0 and self-hosted, with an optional paid cloud mirror for cross-device sync.

evidence.title: Show HN: CMEM – Persistent Memory for AI Coding Agents

entries.title: Agentic Context Management treats memory as a lifecycle, not a store
entries.html:
The ACM paper argues production agents fail less from weak reasoning than from unmanaged context: histories, large prompts, tool definitions, and ballooning tool outputs. It names five primitives (architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, compacting and consolidation) and ships a reference implementation, Maximem Synap.

It puts a shape on the cost curve: naive accumulation grows token cost quadratically with conversation length, crude summarization buys linear cost with an accuracy cliff, and only validated compaction gets linear cost with fidelity preserved. See context compaction.

evidence.title: Agentic Context Management: Solving Agent Memory and Cost by Treating Them as Lifecycle and Architecture Problems

also.title: Agent token costs are unpredictable and easily run away

entries.title: PRO-LONG searches a full interaction log with code and gains 18 points on ARC-AGI-3
entries.html:
PRO-LONG keeps a complete, structured interaction log instead of summarizing or pruning it, and has a coding agent search that log programmatically rather than by embedding similarity.

On the full ARC-AGI-3 public game set it improves 18.0 percentage points over a base coding agent and matches or beats specialized long-horizon harnesses (up to 76.1% pass@1) while using 4.2-5.8x fewer tokens. Memory retrieval becomes a code-search problem.

evidence.title: PRO-LONG: Programmatic Memory Enables Long-Horizon Reasoning

entries.title: Postgres as the agent memory layer: JSONB, HNSW vectors, and row-level locking
entries.html:
Gwen Shapira's talk uses PostgreSQL to give agents both deterministic context (JSONB) and semantic context (high-recall HNSW vector indexes), with vector quantization speeding queries 4x, plus strategies for managing agentic memory.

For multiple agents writing shared notes and decisions, Postgres's own ACID transactions and row-level locking prevent write conflicts without a purpose-built memory service. It applies the "ride infrastructure you already run" instinct to the write-conflict problem.

evidence.title: Presentation: Postgres for Production Agents: Your Relational Foundation for Enterprise AI

also.title: Agent infrastructure buckles under concurrency, not just load

entries.title: OpenWiki Brains turns Gmail, Notion, and git into a local Markdown wiki for proactive recall
entries.html:
OpenWiki Brains turns sources such as Gmail, Notion, git repos, X, Hacker News, and web search into a local wiki of plain Markdown files that agents read as fresh memory.

The memory layer is synthesized Markdown refreshed by scheduled jobs, not a vector index. Recall is proactive: the agent draws on it without being told to remember, unlike the reactive "remember this" pattern most assistants ship.

evidence.title: OpenWiki Brains: Proactive Memory for AI Agents

entries.title: FARMA poisons an agent's remembered reasoning, not just its stored facts
entries.html:
The Forged Amplifying Rationale Memory Attack (FARMA) targets an agent's stored reasoning history. It inserts forged reasoning traces in evasive language that bypasses keyword-based defenses, then amplifies them; the paper also studies defenses.

Memory poisoning extends from corrupting what an agent believes to corrupting how it argues for it. Any memory that stores rationales or tool-use history needs the same provenance controls as stored facts.

evidence.title: Your Agent's Memories Are Not Its Own: Forged Reasoning Attacks on LLM Agent Memory and Defenses

also.title: Untrusted input and tools can hijack an agent

entries.title: One email can plant a hidden memory that a personal agent acts on but never mentions
entries.html:
"When Claws Remember but Do Not Tell" studies stealth memory injection in persistent personal agents. A remote black-box attacker sends a single email payload that must get the agent to write poisoned memory, stay hidden from the user in the agent's replies, and steer future behavior.

The planted entry need not look false, only concealed, so write-time checks aimed at obviously wrong facts may not flag it. Untrusted external content written to memory becomes trusted state later.

evidence.title: When Claws Remember but Do Not Tell: Stealthy Memory Injection in Persistent Personal Agents

also.title: Untrusted input and tools can hijack an agent

entries.title: codebase-memory-mcp exposes a repository's memory to coding agents over MCP
entries.html:
codebase-memory-mcp serves a codebase's memory to coding agents over MCP, reported to speed up agent queries against the repo.

It is the "memory over MCP" shape of Elastic's Atlas, scoped to one repository instead of an enterprise platform.

evidence.title: codebase-memory-mcp speeds AI coding agent queries - Let's Data Science

also.title: Model Context Protocol: a standard interface for agent tools

entries.title: MemSyco-Bench: retrieved memories push agents toward telling users what they want to hear
entries.html:
MemSyco-Bench measures sycophancy induced by memory: retrieved memories cause agents to over-align with the user at the cost of factual accuracy or objective reasoning. Existing memory benchmarks check whether memories are stored and retrieved correctly, not how they bend downstream decisions.

This is harder to catch than a false fact, because it looks like the memory system working as intended.

evidence.title: MemSyco-Bench: Benchmarking Sycophancy in Agent Memory

entries.title: Knotic layers coding-agent memory into project, session, and docs tiers
entries.html:
Knotic gives AI coding agents layered memory split into project, session, and docs tiers.

It is the tiered reference architecture showing up bottom-up at single-developer scale, the same split LinkedIn and Elastic describe for enterprise platforms.

evidence.title: Show HN: Knotic – layered memory (project/session/docs) for AI coding agents

entries.title: AgenticSTS frames long-horizon memory as a contract about what each decision may see
entries.html:
AgenticSTS is a testbed for long-horizon agent memory. Its bounded contract builds every decision from a fresh message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended, so the prompt stays bounded across runs of any length.

Appending everything makes past context easy to reach but leaves the effect of any single memory component impossible to isolate. A bounded contract makes memory components measurable one at a time.

evidence.title: AgenticSTS: A Bounded-Memory Testbed for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

entries.title: Sibyl shares one self-hosted memory across many parallel coding agents
entries.html:
Sibyl is a self-hosted, multi-user memory system built on SurrealDB that many parallel coding agents read and write through a CLI (the author finds it works better than MCP) or MCP. It started as a Kanban board for agents with a crawler and RAG.

It reports 96.96% strict recall@5 on LongMemEval-S with no LLM in the retrieval path: a shared, developer-owned substrate can serve many concurrent agents and stay cheap to query.

evidence.title: Show HN: Sibyl – self-hosted cross-agent memory for AI coding agents

entries.title: Practitioners say agent memory is leaving the "remember this" demo phase
entries.html:
A widely shared practitioner post argues agent memory is leaving the "remember this" demo phase and turning into a real engineering layer.

It landed the same week Elastic open-sourced Atlas, and it marks the shift this page tracks: the question is no longer whether an agent should have memory but what to write, when, and how to recall it cheaply.

evidence.title: Agent memory is leaving the cute "remember this" demo phase

entries.title: Supafax uses the user's email outbox as an agent's memory and config store
entries.html:
Supafax is an agent that uses email as its memory. You email yourself to talk to it; it treats that slice of your outbox as its inbox and short-term memory, and it inserts emails into your inbox to store routines, reminders, and rules for itself.

The builders pick email because it is an append-only, immutable record. The catch they name: users are reluctant to hand that data to a company.

evidence.title: Show HN: I built an agent that uses email as a file system

entries.title: Elastic open-sources Atlas, three-tier agent memory on Elasticsearch over MCP
entries.html:
Elastic's Atlas maintains three categories of agent memory on top of Elasticsearch, integrates with agents over MCP, and keeps each user's memories isolated. On question answering it scored 0.89 Recall@10.

It is an open, production-grade instance of the tiered model, built on infrastructure many teams already run, and it ships evaluation numbers rather than a demo.

evidence.title: Elastic Open-Sources Atlas Agent Memory Based on Cognitive Science

entries.title: A benchmark targets the failure modes of agent memory, not just recall accuracy
entries.html:
A new open benchmark scores the failure modes of agent memory: forgetting, stale recall, poisoning, and retrieval that returns the wrong slice.

It turns "did the memory layer help" into a number you can regress on, the trajectory evaluation already took with agent benchmarks.

evidence.title: Show HN: A benchmark for the failure modes of agent memory

entries.title: LangChain's memory guide adds trace analysis on top of the short-term/long-term split
entries.html:
LangChain's practical guide to agent memory lays out short-term and long-term memory as settled practice, then adds a feedback loop: analyze the agent's own traces in LangSmith to decide what is worth remembering and to improve across runs.

Memory becomes something the agent curates from its own history, not just a place facts get dumped.

evidence.title: How to Build Memory into AI Agents

entries.title: An S3-backed durable filesystem syncs agent memory files across laptop and cloud
entries.html:
A developer built an S3-based durable filesystem, in Rust with Python and TypeScript SDKs and a CLI, that mounts anywhere so the memory Markdown files agents write on a laptop and in the cloud stay in sync.

It treats the memory store as a portable substrate that follows the agent between runtimes, the build-it-yourself answer to the cross-platform consistency managed services sell.

evidence.title: Show HN: A durable filesystem layer for AI agents

entries.title: Similarity search misses logically relevant memories; Root Memories benchmarks the gap
entries.html:
"Towards Root Memories" shows that memory retrieval based on semantic similarity misses memories that are logically critical but share little wording with the query. It builds IMLogic, a benchmark for implicit logical memory retrieval in long dialogues, and proposes root memory, a structured, decision-preserving representation of reusable personal facts.

The recall step has to reason over what is stored, not just embed and rank. See vector/graph retrieval.

evidence.title: Towards Root Memories: Benchmarking and Enhancing Implicit Logical Memory Retrieval for Personalized LLMs

also.title: External knowledge base: vector and graph retrieval

entries.title: Agent memory systems readily admit poisoned facts, a reproducible benchmark shows
entries.html:
A reproducible benchmark shows agent-memory systems readily admit poisoned facts: adversarial or wrong entries that are written once and then retrieved as trusted context on every later turn.

Persistent memory is a persistent attack surface. Write-time validation and provenance become part of the memory-engineering job, not just recall quality. See prompt injection.

evidence.title: Agent-memory systems admit poisoned facts – a reproducible benchmark

also.title: Untrusted input and tools can hijack an agent

entries.title: PMB pairs BM25, vectors, and an entity graph in local memory for coding agents
entries.html:
PMB stores memory in one SQLite file plus a local LanceDB vector index, with no server, cloud service, or API keys. Retrieval fuses BM25, vector search, and an entity co-occurrence graph with reciprocal rank fusion; the stated goal is the right memory, not the closest one.

It hooks the agent lifecycle over MCP: relevant memories are injected before each response, and decisions and learnings are recorded after each turn without manual saves.

evidence.title: Show HN: PMB – local-first memory for AI coding agents over MCP

entries.title: FERNme builds graph memory with ~zero LLM calls using a Hebbian co-occurrence rule
entries.html:
FERNme is a graph-based associative memory that forms memory tags from fuzzy edges and a Hebbian co-occurrence rule, updating with roughly zero LLM calls.

It is the cheap-writes pattern: build the memory structure deterministically instead of asking a model what to store each turn, so persisting what an agent learns stops being a per-turn token bill.

evidence.title: Show HN: FERNme – agent memory that updates with ~zero LLM calls

entries.title: Memharness puts bi-temporal agent memory in one SQLite file
entries.html:
Memharness stores agent memory bi-temporally in a single SQLite file: it tracks both when a fact was true and when the agent learned it.

That lets recall reason about staleness instead of returning whatever embeds nearest. Richer temporal modeling is a recurring design choice in the local-first stores.

evidence.title: Show HN: Memharness – Bi-temporal memory for AI agents, in one SQLite file

entries.title: Cortex offers local-first, encrypted agent memory over MCP
entries.html:
Cortex is a local-first, encrypted memory store for AI agents, written in Rust and exposed over MCP.

It is an early entrant in the developer-owned wave: memory you install and keep on your machine, with encryption at rest, rather than a hosted service.

evidence.title: Show HN: Cortex – local-first encrypted memory for AI agents (Rust, MCP)

entries.title: Brain2.0 gives Claude Code curated, file-based project memory
entries.html:
Project Brain2.0 provides curated project memory for Claude Code and any agent that can read files.

The store is plain files, so it needs no server and works with any file-reading agent. The emphasis on curated memory points at the write side: deciding what belongs in the project record, not only how to retrieve it.

evidence.title: Project Brain2.0–curated project memory for ClaudeCode(+ any file-reading agent)

entries.title: A practitioner survey compares Letta, Mem0, Graphiti, and Cognee as agent memory backends
entries.html:
A practitioner write-up surveys agent memory systems and knowledge graphs through four open projects: Letta, Mem0, Graphiti, and Cognee.

For teams choosing a memory layer, these four are the usual starting shortlist, and they differ mainly in whether memory is organized as a store of facts or as a knowledge graph.

evidence.title: Agent Memory Systems and Knowledge Graphs: Letta, Mem0, Graphiti, and Cognee

entries.title: LinkedIn's Cognitive Memory Agent splits memory into episodic, semantic, and procedural layers
entries.html:
LinkedIn's Cognitive Memory Agent (CMA) is an infrastructure layer that gives agents persistent memory across episodic, semantic, and procedural layers, with support for multi-agent coordination, retrieval, and lifecycle management.

It is a useful reference architecture for the tiered split: working context, a log of past interactions, and durable facts and procedures. It also treats memory as shared platform infrastructure for many agents, not a per-agent prompt feature.

evidence.title: Designing Memory for AI Agents: Inside Linkedin’s Cognitive Memory Agent

entries.title: Stream processing with Kafka and Flink drives dynamic memory tiering for agents
entries.html:
Adi Polak's talk on context engineering and memory management uses Apache Kafka and Flink for real-time stream processing, dynamic memory tiering, and tool orchestration over MCP, aimed at token limits, cost spikes, and latency.

It frames the move from stateless prompts to state-aware agents as a distributed-systems problem. Teams already running streaming infrastructure can build the memory tiers on it rather than adopting a new store.

evidence.title: Presentation: Beyond Prompting: Context Engineering and Memory Management for AI Systems at Scale

also.title: Context compaction: summarize, compress, and curate the working set

entries.title: Cloudflare launches Agent Memory, a managed persistent memory service
entries.html:
Cloudflare's Agent Memory, in private beta, extracts structured memories from agent conversations and retrieves them on demand with five-channel parallel retrieval fused by Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Shared memory profiles let teams of agents read common knowledge. It competes with Mem0, Zep, LangMem, and Letta.

This is the buy side of the build-vs-buy split: memory as rented infrastructure next to your edge compute.

evidence.title: Cloudflare Announces Agent Memory, a Managed Persistent Memory Service for AI Agents

agent-observability.title: You can't see why an agent did what it did
agent-observability.summary:
When an agent does the wrong thing, the run behind it is a long,
non-deterministic chain of model calls, tool results, and intermediate
decisions, and most of it is invisible afterwards. Unlike a stack trace, an
agent's "why" is spread across a trajectory you didn't log in enough detail,
can't replay deterministically, and can't easily diff against a working run.

sections.heading: TL;DR
sections.html: When an agent does the wrong thing, the run behind it is a long, non-deterministic chain of model calls, tool results, and intermediate decisions, and most of it is invisible afterwards. Unlike a stack trace, an agent's "why" is spread across a trajectory you didn't log in enough detail, can't replay deterministically, and can't easily diff against a working run.

sections.heading: State of the art
sections.html:
Observability for agents is trace-first. The unit captured is the full trajectory: prompts, tool calls, results, retries, and subagent handoffs. Harnesses and serving platforms now emit these spans natively over OpenTelemetry, and capture extends to voice agents and plain CLIs.

The bottleneck has moved from capture to reading. Teams run a model over the traces to surface recurring failure patterns, debug many coding agents in one console, and read a session as a single thread instead of a span tree. Loops and runaway spend show up in the same trace, so trace and cost views are merging.

Agentic root-cause analysis works with guardrails, not alone. Production systems pair pre-correlated telemetry with LLM analysis and keep a human approving changes. Evidence suggests models can reason about a failure once the context is assembled. The best frontier agent on a realistic oncall benchmark still gets only about a quarter of root causes right, so the pipeline, not the model, is the open problem.

Ownership is a design choice. Enterprises want traces and spend data in their own network, through a self-hosted gateway or a managed platform deployed into their cloud. Payload privacy defaults differ by framework, and traces can be truncated.

The trace has limits. Offline monitoring covers agents you can't watch live, and agents can coordinate through hidden states a transcript never records. Evaluating the monitors is itself an evaluation problem.

sections.heading: Why it matters for platform engineers
sections.html:
You cannot operate what you cannot explain. Without trajectory-level traces, a regression after a model upgrade, a silent tool failure, or a runaway loop stays invisible until it shows up as cost or a user complaint, and you can't reproduce it.

Observability is the precondition for the rest of the stack: evaluation needs traces to grade, cost control needs per-step attribution, and incident response needs a replayable run. The build-vs-buy choice is whether to standardize on a trace format and own the analysis, or adopt a managed platform. Either way, check payload retention and truncation defaults: the trace is the new log line, and it carries secrets.

themes.title: Capturing the full trajectory
themes.summary: Harnesses, serving platforms, and CLIs now emit agent spans natively over OpenTelemetry, across text and voice, but payload defaults, truncation, and retention vary by tool.

themes.title: Making traces readable and analyzable
themes.summary: Capture is no longer the bottleneck; models now read traces to surface failure patterns, and viewers present a session as one readable thread instead of a span tree.

themes.title: Agents doing root-cause analysis and on-call
themes.summary: Production RCA and triage agents work when telemetry is pre-correlated and a human approves changes; benchmarks show end-to-end oncall accuracy is still low.

themes.title: Where agent telemetry lives
themes.summary: Enterprises want traces and spend data inside their own network, answered either by self-hosted gateways or by managed platforms deployed into the customer's cloud.

themes.title: When the trace is not enough
themes.summary: Offline monitoring covers agents you cannot instrument live, and latent-channel work shows a complete transcript can still miss how agents coordinated.

entries.title: LangSmith Trajectories shows an agent session as one readable thread, not a span tree
entries.html:
LangSmith's Trajectories renders a whole agent session as a conversational thread: user turns, tool calls, and subagent handoffs read top to bottom, instead of the nested span tree a generic OpenTelemetry viewer shows.

It trades completeness of the tree for the job that bottlenecks debugging long-running agents: scanning a session fast enough to spot where it went wrong.

evidence.title: Trajectories now in LangSmith: A readable view of every agent session

entries.title: Session traces and cost controls converge into one agent-failure diagnostic
entries.html:
InfoQ coverage of agent observability practice treats tool-call loops and runaway spend as the same triage step: both show up in the same session trace, and both need enough preserved execution context for post-incident debugging.

Cost dashboards and trace viewers are one diagnostic surface. See cost controls.

evidence.title: Session Traces and Cost Controls Help Diagnose AI Agent Failures

entries.title: Figma's security agents resolve complex alerts 70% faster, with memory as the main lever
entries.html:
Figma built alert-triage agents on a Panther SIEM foundation, querying 100+ data sources (AWS, Okta, GitHub, GCP, osquery) and scoped to the tools an on-call engineer uses. The team reports memory, not model choice or tool count, as the biggest quality lever.

Reported results: 70% faster resolution on complex alerts, 20% fewer on-call pages from re-tuned severity, and 100+ previously unknown vulnerabilities found. Agent-authored PRs default to draft and every fix needs human approval.

evidence.title: How Figma Uses AI Agents for Security

entries.title: OpenSearch MCP Apps return trace waterfalls and service maps inline in the agent chat
entries.html:
Amazon OpenSearch Service's MCP Apps return an interactive visualization alongside each tool call's text response. A local MCP server authenticates with AWS credentials, queries the same OpenSearch and Prometheus sources behind existing dashboards, and renders the result inline in the IDE.

One conversation moves from alert to log clustering, trace waterfalls, and service maps without opening a separate tool. MCP carries the observability payload itself.

evidence.title: Agentic observability with Amazon OpenSearch Service MCP Apps

entries.title: Pond archives agent sessions losslessly to your own S3 bucket and serves them over MCP
entries.html:
Pond, a Show HN project, stores agent sessions from multiple machines in one S3 bucket you own, with no database service to run. Sessions are searchable and exposed to the agent as an MCP server.

Session history becomes a durable, portable record under the team's control rather than local files tied to one laptop or tool.

evidence.title: Show HN: Pond – lossless archive for agent sessions in your own S3

entries.title: Agents can coordinate through hidden states a full transcript never shows
entries.html:
Language-model agents can communicate through continuous hidden states invisible in public transcripts. Verifiable Latent Alignments (VLA) links each private latent-state record and channel status to the resulting public action through a shared event identifier, and layers representation anomaly detection on top.

A complete trace of what agents said can still miss what they communicated. In multi-agent systems, message-and-tool-call spans are the wrong unit when coordination happens below the message layer.

evidence.title: Beyond the Transcript: Detecting Covert Co ordination in Latent Multi-Agent Communication

entries.title: Cloudflare adds native agent tracing, with truncated payloads and opposite privacy defaults
entries.html:
Cloudflare added agent spans to existing Workers traces: invoke_agent, chat/execute_tool, and tool_approval, keyed by agent name, agent ID, and conversation ID, so a session replays turn by turn.

The gotchas are concrete:

  • Payload recording defaults differ by framework: off under Vercel's AI SDK, on under Flue. Those payloads often carry personal data or secrets.
  • Traces are not lossless; payloads may be truncated, dropping the arguments a debug session needs.
  • From October 1, 2026, every span is a billable event.

evidence.title: Cloudflare Adds Agent Tracing, with Truncation Limits and Uneven Payload Defaults

entries.title: Simon Willison's LLM 0.32 logs visible reasoning traces in redesigned SQLite logs
entries.html:
LLM 0.32, the biggest release of the CLI since launch, adds visible reasoning traces, server-side provider tools, and redesigned content-addressable SQLite logs, plus features from the OpenAI Responses API.

Trajectory capture is available in a widely used, framework-agnostic command-line tool, not only in hosted platforms.

evidence.title: New release of LLM adds support for reasoning traces, OpenAI Responses, server-side tools, and smarter logging

entries.title: LangSmith Bring Your Own Cloud reaches GA on AWS
entries.html:
LangSmith's Bring Your Own Cloud option is generally available on AWS, giving enterprise teams managed observability, evaluation, and deployment inside their own VPC.

It meets the "keep traces in our network" requirement from the vendor side: the Claude Apps Gateway answers it by self-hosting, BYOC by deploying the managed product into the customer's cloud.

evidence.title: LangSmith BYOC on AWS is generally available

entries.title: LangChain's Kubernetes SRE agent needs human approval and records every step in traces
entries.html:
LangChain built an autonomous SRE agent for Kubernetes on Deep Agents. It requires human approval before applying a change, and every step, tool call, and decision is captured in LangSmith traces and covered by evals.

The trace is what a human reviews before the agent acts, not only what an engineer replays afterward.

evidence.title: How we built an autonomous SRE agent for Kubernetes

entries.title: ORCA-bench: the best frontier agent gets 25.3% of realistic oncall root causes right
entries.html:
ORCA-bench pairs an OpenTelemetry-instrumented microservice testbed (six days of metrics, logs, and traces) with 1,079 oncall RCA tasks, graded by an LLM judge that human SREs re-scored (κ=0.90). Across five frontier agents, the best accuracy is 25.3% on realistic-input tasks and 10.0% on hard ones. The weakest model invents an implausible root cause on 40% of reports.

The authors read this as a lower bound on the real-world gap. The reasoning may be there, but the end-to-end oncall pipeline is mostly unsolved.

evidence.title: ORCA-bench: How Ready Are Language Model Agents for Oncall?

entries.title: Indie observability tools for coding agents keep appearing beside the vendors
entries.html:
A Show HN project ships observability for coding agents and LLM applications.

It is one more self-hostable option in the trace-first tooling space, alongside the managed platforms.

evidence.title: Show HN: Observability for Coding Agents and LLM Applications

entries.title: Coroot experiment: LLMs can do RCA once the telemetry context is prepared
entries.html:
A Coroot experiment running root-cause analysis across eleven models offers early evidence that modern LLMs can reason through RCA once given correctly prepared context.

The hard problem moves from model reasoning to the pipelines that correlate telemetry into that context, the work Expedia's STAR invests in.

evidence.title: AI Root Cause Analysis Shifts from Model Reasoning to Context Engineering

entries.title: Expedia's STAR turns live telemetry into root-cause assessments with engineers in the loop
entries.html:
Expedia's STAR, built on FastAPI, Datadog, Celery, Redis, and Langfuse, ingests service telemetry during incidents, runs structured workflows to generate root-cause assessments, and keeps engineers in the loop for the final call.

It is the trace-plus-LLM-analysis pattern built on infrastructure a platform team already runs, not a new observability product.

evidence.title: Expedia Uses AI Driven Service Telemetry Analyzer to Accelerate Incident Investigation

entries.title: LangSmith traces voice agents, including audio, STT/TTS latency, and interruptions
entries.html:
LangSmith now traces voice agents built on Pipecat, LiveKit, OpenAI Realtime, and Gemini Live, capturing audio, STT and TTS latency, interruptions, and tool calls in one trace.

Trajectory capture extends to the turn-taking and latency failures specific to spoken interfaces. See agent latency for why voice has a harder real-time floor.

evidence.title: Trace voice agents in LangSmith

entries.title: AWS's Claude Apps Gateway relays telemetry and enforces spend caps from a self-hosted container
entries.html:
AWS and Anthropic released the Claude Apps Gateway, a single stateless container an organization runs in front of Claude Code and Claude Desktop. It centralizes identity, policy, routing, and telemetry, relays per-request usage metrics to the team's own OpenTelemetry collector (CloudWatch, Prometheus), and enforces YAML-defined spend caps by org, group, or user.

Telemetry relay and cost policy live in one customer-owned layer instead of a vendor dashboard.

evidence.title: AWS Ships Claude Apps Gateway as Self-Hosted Control Plane for Claude Code and Claude Desktop

entries.title: LangSmith traces Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Copilot in one debug console
entries.html:
LangSmith now positions itself as the debug console for any coding agent: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and more. One view shows tool calls, subagent handoffs, errors, cost, and retries.

Which agent produced a trace becomes a detail the observability layer abstracts away, instead of a reason to read each tool's own logs.

evidence.title: How to Debug Coding Agents with LangSmith Traces

entries.title: Schneider Electric unifies observability, evaluation, and deployment on LangSmith
entries.html:
Schneider Electric built its enterprise LLMOps foundations on LangSmith to unify observability, evaluation, and deployment for AI products at scale (vendor case study).

It is an enterprise deployment of the trace as the shared substrate for ops and eval, not just a vendor pitch for it.

evidence.title: How Schneider Electric Built Their LLMOps Foundations With LangSmith

entries.title: Claude Code tags workflow-spawned agents with OpenTelemetry run IDs
entries.html:
claude-code v2.1.202 adds workflow.run_id and workflow.name OpenTelemetry attributes to telemetry from workflow-spawned agents, so a workflow run's activity can be reconstructed from OTel data.

A multi-agent run becomes traceable through the OTel pipeline a team already operates, with no bespoke exporter.

evidence.title: claude-code v2.1.202

entries.title: Offline monitoring evaluates internal agents from logged activity after the fact
entries.html:
"Evaluating Offline Monitoring of Internal AI Agents" studies monitoring agents from logged activity after the run, rather than with live instrumentation.

This matters when runtime tracing is incomplete or the agent runs where you can't watch it. The open question is how good such monitors are, which is itself an evaluation problem.

evidence.title: Evaluating Offline Monitoring of Internal AI Agents

entries.title: LangSmith adds an on-call copilot that triages alerts from agent traces
entries.html:
LangChain's June newsletter announces a Fleet on-call copilot for alert triage in LangSmith, plus voice trace debugging and experiment status tracking.

"Read the traces and tell me what's breaking" becomes a managed agentic product rather than a dashboard.

evidence.title: June 2026: LangChain Newsletter — Fleet On-Call Copilot, Deep Agents Rubrics, and More

entries.title: HALO runs a model over agent traces to find recurring harness-level failure modes
entries.html:
HALO is an open-source local debugger that ingests Langfuse, Arize/OpenInference, or JSONL traces and uses an RLM-based engine to find recurring harness-level failure modes. It produces reports you can feed into Cursor or Claude Code to patch the agent, and a desktop app answers questions over the traces.

The engineer stops reading every span: a model reads the traces and the human reviews the patterns.

evidence.title: Show HN: RLM-based local debugger for AI agent traces

entries.title: A multi-dataset benchmark grades how LLM agents reason through microservice failures
entries.html:
A new benchmark for AgentOps evaluates LLM agents on microservice failure diagnosis over multimodal observability data. It adds two large datasets because existing benchmarks score only the final answer and ignore the reasoning process.

Grading whether an agent diagnosed a failure correctly is a trajectory-grading problem, so agent observability and evaluation converge on the trace.

evidence.title: A Multi-Dataset Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agents in Microservice Failure Diagnosis
