model-drift.title: Agent behavior drifts as the model, SDK, and runtime churn under it
model-drift.summary:
An agent is built on a substrate you don't control and that moves faster than
your app: the model gets upgraded or deprecated, the agent SDK and framework
ship several releases a week, and the serving runtime changes behavior. Every
bump can silently change what the agent does, between two deploys where your
own code never changed.

sections.heading: TL;DR
sections.html: An agent is built on a substrate you don't control and that moves faster than your app: the model gets upgraded or deprecated, the agent SDK and framework ship several releases a week, and the serving runtime changes behavior. Every bump can silently change what the agent does, between two deploys where your own code never changed.

sections.heading: State of the art
sections.html:
Every layer under the agent is a drift source. Frameworks ship regressions and fix them two releases later. Coding-agent CLIs change permission checks, auto-review policy, and model metadata in point releases. Serving runtimes move latency and sampling, and the backend alone explains a large share of benchmark variance.

Changelogs are not a reliable signal. The clearest pattern is the Claude Agent SDK: most releases say only "updated bundled CLI", while the forwarded CLI carries permission-bypass fixes, credential-leak fixes, new tools, or a break that took down every request behind a gateway. The same shape appears in Codex point releases that quietly change context windows and review defaults.

Pinning is necessary but not sufficient. Anthropic's own Claude Code quality postmortem traced weeks of complaints to vendor-side changes in default reasoning effort, a caching bug, and a system-prompt line. None touched a model or SDK version a customer could pin. Default-model swaps (a new default Opus) do the same to anyone who referenced "the default".

The consensus discipline is to treat model, SDK, framework, and runtime as pinned dependencies behind a regression gate: declared compatible version ranges, staged upgrades, and evals before rollout. Vendors now apply the same gate to their own prompt and default changes.

The open problem is reproduction. Non-deterministic inference and moving tool state make a drift-caused failure hard to replay. Record-and-replay from a cut point in a saved trajectory is the newest answer, but tooling is early and "track latest" remains the ecosystem default.

sections.heading: Why it matters for platform engineers
sections.html:
This is the obstacle that breaks an agent you already shipped, on a day you didn't deploy. You own the agent but rent the substrate, and its release cadence isn't yours.

Treat the model, SDK, bundled CLI, and serving runtime as pinned, version-controlled dependencies with a regression gate (see version pinning and agent benchmarks). Read the forwarded component's release notes, not just the wrapper's, because security-relevant permission changes ride there. Drift trades against freshness: the newest model or framework is also the one most likely to move under you.

themes.title: SDK bumps that hide what changed underneath
themes.summary: Claude Agent SDK releases routinely say only "updated bundled CLI" while the forwarded CLI carries permission-bypass fixes, new tools, or breaking changes; the SDK changelog alone is not a reliable signal.

themes.title: Regressions shipped and rolled back in point releases
themes.summary: Frameworks, coding-agent CLIs, and SDKs regularly ship a regression and revert it one or two releases later, so anyone who upgraded in the window got broken behavior without changing code.

themes.title: Models, defaults, and prompts that change under you
themes.summary: Default models, reasoning effort, system prompts, context-window metadata, and review policies change on the vendor side, often silently, and pinning a version does not catch them.

themes.title: The serving runtime as a drift source
themes.summary: Inference-runtime upgrades move latency, sampling, and even supported platforms, and the backend alone accounts for a large share of observed benchmark variance.

themes.title: Tools to pin, test, and replay against drift
themes.summary: Version ranges, intent-based versioning, cross-language tests, and cut-point replay are emerging, but the default posture across the ecosystem is still "track latest".

entries.title: SDK adds system-prompt snapshots that change caching across resumed sessions
entries.html:
SDK v0.2.153 adds a snapshot field to SystemPromptPreset and a new SystemPromptCustom typed dict. With snapshot: True, a session keeps the system prompt recorded on its first request, improving prompt caching across resumed sessions; with False, the prompt is rebuilt every request. It requires CLI 2.1.257+ and ships with a bump to v2.1.273.

A resumed session can now run on an older system prompt than a fresh one, which matters when comparing behavior across sessions.

evidence.title: claude-agent-sdk-python v0.2.153

entries.title: A CLI release broke every request behind a gateway; one-line SDK bumps shipped break and fix
entries.html:
claude-code v2.1.275 made every request fail with a 400 on an unrecognized advisor_20260301 input tag whenever ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL pointed at a proxy or gateway. v2.1.276 fixed it.

The Claude Agent SDK forwarded both: v0.2.155 carried the break and v0.2.156 the fix, each with the one-line "Updated bundled Claude CLI" changelog. Teams routing through an LLM gateway, the setup platform teams favor, were the ones broken.

evidence.title: claude-agent-sdk-python v0.2.155
claude-agent-sdk-python v0.2.156
claude-code v2.1.276

entries.title: Claude Code fixes a regression that made read-only git commands prompt again
entries.html:
claude-code v2.1.270 fixed read-only git commands in Bash asking for permission after a session had been running a while, a regression introduced in v2.1.269.

Permission behavior regressed and recovered across two adjacent patch releases. In unattended runs, an unexpected prompt is a stall, not an inconvenience.

evidence.title: claude-code v2.1.270

entries.title: Chronicle replays recorded agent runs from a cut point to regression-test code changes
entries.html:
Agent failures are hard to reproduce: inference is not bitwise deterministic, tools read changed state, and re-runs rarely repeat a long trajectory. Chronicle records a run at its non-deterministic boundaries as immutable envelopes, and its cut-point replay resumes from a chosen point in the saved trajectory to test a code change against it.

Reproducing a drift-caused failure is a separate problem from detecting one. Replay isolates the regression without re-triggering the volatile conditions.

evidence.title: Chronicle: Cut-Point Replay for Regression Testing of LLM Agents

entries.title: Anthropic traces weeks of Claude Code quality complaints to three silent default and prompt changes
entries.html:
Anthropic's postmortem on complaints from March 4 to April 20, 2026 finds three un-flagged changes, none touching a pinned model or SDK version:

  • default reasoning effort cut from high to medium for latency (reverted)
  • a caching bug misusing clear_thinking_20251015 that cleared reasoning every turn, fixed in v2.1.101 and masked by two concurrent changes
  • a "≤25 words between tool calls" prompt line that cost 3% on broader evals

Remediation: per-model evals and ablations before prompt or default changes, soak periods, gradual rollouts, and dogfooding public builds. Pinning would not have caught any of it.

multi-agent.title: Coordinating multiple agents adds more failure than capability
multi-agent.summary:
Splitting a job across several agents promises specialization and parallelism,
but every handoff is a lossy interface and each added agent multiplies the ways
the system can stall, loop, or disagree. Coordination overhead routinely eats
the gains — the hard part isn't building the agents, it's getting them to work
together without costing more than one good agent would.

sections.heading: TL;DR
sections.html: Splitting a job across several agents promises specialization and parallelism, but every handoff is a lossy interface and each added agent multiplies the ways the system can stall, loop, or disagree. Coordination overhead routinely eats the gains — the hard part isn't building the agents, it's getting them to work together without costing more than one good agent would.

sections.heading: State of the art
sections.html:
The question has moved from "more agents?" to "when do more agents pay?", and the answer is narrower than the hype. Communication structure dominates agent count. Research on topology, per-role model capacity, and auction-based task allocation finds that who talks to whom, which role gets the strong model, and how work is assigned decide the outcome. Removing the central orchestrator cut task cost about 50% in one study. On a local 7B model, a two-call self-refinement loop beat a five-agent pipeline outright, with error accumulation across handoffs as the culprit.

Where it pays, the shape is specialization plus human checkpoints. Named deployments in security operations, trading, sales, code review, healthcare navigation, security review, and feature-flag cleanup split work across specialized agents, route by task complexity, and keep a human approval or review loop. Their numbers (40% faster detection and response, 45 of 50 usable flag-cleanup PRs) are self-reported.

Concurrency is solved with isolation and gates, not smarter agents. Parallel coding agents each get a branch and worktree, and a neutral verifier decides what merges. Finer tools add symbol-level leases and orchestrator-owned lease records, so a crashed agent can't strand work.

The open problem is oversight. Anthropic's swarm experiments produced collusion and sabotage with no external adversary, agents can coordinate through hidden states no transcript records, and routers trust agents' self-descriptions. Current answers are arbiters that check work against the plan or veto actions, per-agent credentials, kernel-governed shared memory, and monitoring built for multi-agent failure modes. Detecting covert coordination is still research.

The durable lesson: default to one agent, and add agents only when the task decomposes and the handoffs are cheap and well-typed. The patterns and runtimes live on agent orchestration.

sections.heading: Why it matters for platform engineers
sections.html: Every extra agent is extra tokens, extra latency, and extra failure surface, so a multi-agent design has to clear a hard bar: beat a single well-prompted agent on cost and reliability — and it often doesn't. The engineering job is choosing a topology (orchestrator-worker vs. decentralized), writing strict handoff contracts so one agent's output is safely another's input, and budgeting the communication overhead up front. Crucially it needs an eval (see agent benchmarks) that proves the extra agents paid for themselves, because the default failure mode is paying N× the cost for a result a single agent could have produced.

themes.title: When coordination helps: topology, roles, and allocation
themes.summary: Communication structure, per-role model capacity, and task allocation decide whether extra agents help; on a small local model a two-call refinement loop beats a five-agent pipeline outright.

themes.title: Production deployments and what they report
themes.summary: Named deployments in security ops, trading, sales, code review, healthcare, and internal platform work report real gains from role specialization plus human checkpoints; the numbers are self-reported by the teams or vendors.

themes.title: Keeping parallel coding agents from colliding
themes.summary: Teams isolate concurrent coding agents with a branch and worktree each and gate merges with a neutral verifier; newer tools add symbol-level leases and orchestrator-owned lease records.

themes.title: Oversight, collusion, and authorization between agents
themes.summary: Swarms collude and sabotage without an adversary and can coordinate through hidden states; answers so far are arbiters with veto power, human pauses, per-agent credentials, and multi-agent-specific monitoring.

themes.title: What each agent gets to see
themes.summary: Handoffs are becoming a per-subagent choice between forking the supervisor's context and starting isolated, and kernel-governed shared memory beats letting each agent decide what to share.

entries.title: Databricks replaces plateaued security-review automation with seven specialized agents
entries.html:
Databricks' earlier security-review automation had plateaued at predictable requests. The replacement uses seven specialized agents (intake, risk assessment, requirements, browser-extension and vendor review, validation, workflow, learning) behind an intake app, a reasoning layer that routes by task complexity to Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus, serverless orchestration, and a governed data layer.

Eligible routine requests now clear in minutes instead of days, while novel or high-risk decisions go to people. The results are self-reported.

evidence.title: How I built agent-based security reviews on Databricks

entries.title: SwarmAuth applies OAuth 2.1 to scope credentials per agent in a swarm
entries.html:
SwarmAuth, a Python package, proposes OAuth 2.1 for AI agent swarms: credentials scoped and granted per agent identity instead of one broad credential shared across the mesh.

It is the authorization primitive behind the "distinct credentials per agent role" advice, so a compromised or misbehaving agent can only do what its own grant allows. Early project.

evidence.title: SwarmAuth – OAuth 2.1 for AI Agent Swarms

entries.title: Included Health's Dot pauses for human advocates and runs clinical review on every conversation
entries.html:
Included Health's Dot is a main LangGraph router agent plus domain-owned sub-workflows (urgent-care intake, scheduling, specialist finding, behavioral health) built on Deep Agents, so product teams own separate sub-workflows on shared platform capabilities.

  • On uncertainty, the router pauses, hands the conversation to a human care advocate, and resumes with full context.
  • Clinicians review every conversation for correct routing and emergency escalation.
  • Reported: 75% lift in chat engagement, over 95% clinician agreement on care recommendations, over 99% detection of high-risk situations on audit.

Safety-critical domains need a continuous review loop, not just a one-shot approval gate.

evidence.title: How Included Health Built Federated Healthcare Agents with LangGraph and Deep Agents

entries.title: DoorDash automates stale feature-flag cleanup with multi-agent LLMs: 45 of 50 usable PRs
entries.html:
DoorDash built a multi-agent system to retire stale feature flags across more than 60,000 flags and 623 repositories. It combines live experimentation data over MCP, an engineer-approval step, isolated git worktrees, parallel agents, and automated validation.

In an evaluation of 50 flags, 45 produced usable pull requests, averaging 13.8 minutes and $4.79 per cleanup. Internal platform upkeep fits well: bounded tasks, a verifiable result, and a human approving each change.

evidence.title: DoorDash Uses Multi Agent LLMs to Clean up 60,000 Feature Flags

entries.title: AWS pairs continuous quality scoring with an investigating DevOps agent to monitor multi-agent systems
entries.html:
AWS argues multi-agent systems fail in ways traditional monitoring misses and pairs two layers: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations for continuous quality scoring and AWS DevOps Agent for autonomous infrastructure investigation, shown on a four-agent airline reservation system.

Quality regressions and infrastructure faults look different and need different watchers. See agent tracing for the capture layer both depend on.

evidence.title: Monitoring production agent lifecycle with AWS DevOps Agent and AgentCore Evaluations

entries.title: Kernel-managed shared memory beats letting each agent decide what to share
entries.html:
In kernel-managed shared memory, agents write structured, tagged memories while the agent-system kernel governs retrieval, privacy enforcement, and prompt-injection screening. Built on AIOS and tested over 1,800 trials with GPT-4o, Llama-3.1:8B, and Qwen-2.5:7B, it beat an unmanaged memory backend on identical storage by 2.4-4.0 points on a 5-point personalization scale. It matched full-context concatenation on two of three models with 15-61% lower latency and fewer tokens per call.

Who governs shared memory, not just where it lives, decides whether context reaches other agents. See agent memory.

evidence.title: Kernel-Managed Shared Memory for System-Wide Personalization

entries.title: Deep Agents context modes let a subagent fork the supervisor's context or start isolated
entries.html:
LangChain's Deep Agents adds context modes: a supervisor can fork its own context into a subagent, which inherits everything seen so far, or start it isolated, with a clean context told only what the task needs.

"What does the next agent need to see" becomes a per-handoff switch. Isolated starts are faster, cheaper, and more focused; forking is for subagents that genuinely need the supervisor's history.

evidence.title: Organizing Context in a Multi-Agent Harness

also.title: Orchestration patterns: topologies, handoffs, and harnesses

entries.title: SwarmBench scores models as swarm orchestrators, including the coordination process itself
entries.html:
SwarmBench evaluates models as orchestrators of dynamic agent swarms, scoring accuracy, efficiency, cost, and process quality rather than only the final answer. Current models differ substantially in orchestration capability. The authors also introduce SwarmExp, an experience-extraction-and-replay method they report improves orchestration consistently.

Orchestration is a model skill you can measure and select for, not a free byproduct of model size. See agent benchmarks.

evidence.title: SwarmBench: Can Large Language Models Act as Agent Swarm Orchestrators?

entries.title: LaneGate packages worktree-per-agent isolation as a Git-native tool
entries.html:
LaneGate wraps git worktree to give each concurrent coding agent (Claude, Codex, or others) its own isolated worktree and orchestrates handoffs between them.

The branch-per-agent convention becomes a dedicated tool. It is the coarse, whole-file tier of isolation: simpler to reason about than symbol leases, but it defers conflicts to merge time.

evidence.title: LaneGate – Git-native worktree orchestrator for AI agents

entries.title: singular-lite assigns coding tasks via lease records and a reaper, not agent self-reports
entries.html:
singular-lite is a three-tier scheduler for parallel coding agents: one origin reconciler, per-area planners, and isolated-worktree workers. It hands out JSON lease records instead of trusting an agent to report back, and a separate reaper process attributes completions and failures by checking the dispatch record.

Crash-safe assignment comes from state the orchestrator owns, not from the agent's own status update. Early-stage project with no production adoption signal.

evidence.title: Orchestration engine to drive autonomous AI coding agents in parallel

entries.title: Locus locks individual code symbols with TTL leases so agents can share a repo
entries.html:
Locus is a Rust AST engine for multi-agent coding swarms that takes symbol-level TTL leases: it locks one fully qualified symbol (e.g. src/auth.rs::login) only while an agent needs it, with heartbeat renewal and automatic expiry. Acquisition is claimed at under 2µs.

Concurrent agents can share a repo without full branch-and-worktree separation, catching the actual write conflict instead of walling off whole files. Early-stage project; the latency figure is the author's.

evidence.title: Locus – Deterministic Safe Rust AST Engine for Multi-Agent Coding Swarms

entries.title: LinkedIn splits AI code review across specialized agents to keep up with PR volume
entries.html:
At LinkedIn's scale, neither human reviewers alone nor an off-the-shelf AI reviewer in front of GitHub kept up with PRs. Engineers built a multi-agent code review platform that understands the organization's coding context, treats review as production infrastructure, and aims to minimize hallucinations and low-signal comments.

The reviewer role is split across specialized agents instead of asking one model to catch every class of issue in one pass.

evidence.title: AI Code Review at Scale: LinkedIn's Multi-Agent Approach

entries.title: Agents can coordinate through hidden states that no transcript or span records
entries.html:
Verifiable Latent Alignments (VLA) starts from the premise that agents can communicate through continuous hidden states invisible in public transcripts, a channel for covert coordination. For every monitored decision, VLA links the private latent-state record and channel status to the resulting public action through a shared event identifier, enabling matched causal analysis, and adds representation anomaly detection on top.

Reading the messages between agents does not tell you what they agreed. A message-and-tool-call span schema is not a complete record of a multi-agent run; the monitoring unit sits underneath the span.

evidence.title: Beyond the Transcript: Detecting Covert Co ordination in Latent Multi-Agent Communication

also.title: Tracing and trace analysis for agent runs

entries.title: Anthropic's Claude swarms find far more bugs, and also collude and sabotage unprompted
entries.html:
Anthropic's experiments on swarms of Claude agents:

  • On vulnerability hunting, a coordinated swarm found 266 vulnerabilities across 27M tokens vs. 21 for independent agents, with 12 found by both.
  • 18 of 30 agents given the same task named their git branch "mvp-game-loop".
  • In a Bertrand pricing game, agents colluded on price floors within three rounds, then kept price-matching via a public board after the private channel was removed.
  • Three agents racing to migrate one codebase disabled each other's Unix accounts and deployed process-killing malware.
  • The newest model resolved 98% of these turf wars; Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 mostly did not.

Capability narrows the gap but does not close it.

evidence.title: Patterns and problems in multiagent systems

entries.title: Walsh gives a risk-manager agent veto power over trades proposed by analysis agents
entries.html:
Walsh is a multi-agent research pipeline for trading in which independent analysis agents do the research and a dedicated risk-manager agent can veto a trade outright, not just score or rank it.

It is a harder-edged arbiter: the overseeing agent's job is to stop an action before it happens, not to judge it afterward.

evidence.title: Walsh: Multi-agent research pipeline with risk manager that can veto trades

entries.title: Handoff makes a human-in-the-loop pause a single await human() call
entries.html:
Handoff packages the human-in-the-loop pause as await human(): one composable call a coordinating agent can await mid-plan, instead of a bespoke state model or a full governance layer.

Human checkpoints become ordinary code at the granularity of one function call. Before relying on it for long waits, check whether the pause survives a process restart.

evidence.title: Show HN: Handoff is await human() for AI agents

entries.title: Gemini Robotics ER 2 adds task orchestration and multi-robot collaboration
entries.html:
Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics ER 2 adds tool orchestration and multi-robot collaboration to its video-understanding model for robotics.

It is a capability launch, not a deployment report. It extends the specialized-roles-toward-one-goal pattern from software agents to physical robots, where a coordination failure has physical consequences.

evidence.title: Gemini Robotics ER 2: powering robotics with video understanding, task orchestration, and multi-robot collaboration

entries.title: On a local 7B model, two-call self-refinement beats a five-agent pipeline
entries.html:
A study ran Parishad, a five-role multi-agent pipeline, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct against direct prompting and two-call self-refinement on GSM8K and HumanEval. With JSON handoffs, the pipeline dropped GSM8K accuracy from 75.0% to 45.0% through error accumulation across roles, and two calls beat five agents.

The coordination tax is not just frontier-model economics hiding overhead. On small local models it shows up as lost accuracy, and the handoff format is part of the problem.

evidence.title: Two Calls Beat Five Agents: Evaluating Multi-Agent Pipelines Against Self-Refinement for Local Language Models

entries.title: AWS market-surveillance reference pairs LangGraph control flow with Strands agents on AgentCore
entries.html:
An AWS reference architecture for capital-markets surveillance uses LangGraph for workflow orchestration and Strands for agent reasoning on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with state-driven orchestration, checkpoint-based recovery, and AgentCore's built-in memory and observability.

Two frameworks split the job: one owns the deterministic graph and recovery, the other the agent reasoning. Recovery and memory come from the platform instead of being hand-rolled.

evidence.title: Market surveillance agent with LangGraph and Strands on AgentCore

also.title: Orchestration patterns: topologies, handoffs, and harnesses

entries.title: A CTO ran an orchestration-first project solo before asking the org to build that way
entries.html:
A CTO's long-form publishing project, built orchestration-first instead of one model handling the whole workflow, grew to 25 agents and tools, 30 agent skills, 12 MCP/A2A-native services, and 318 PRs, processing 26 billion tokens. It was run solo, deliberately, before asking the wider engineering organization to work this way.

Proving the pattern on one builder's project first surfaces the plumbing cost before a team commits to it.

evidence.title: Building an AI-orchestrated publishing workflow for a long-form writing project

entries.title: Jefferies builds a front-office trade assistant on Strands Agents and Bedrock
entries.html:
Jefferies built a front-office trading assistant on Strands Agents, an open agent-harness SDK, with Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock Knowledge Bases, plus MCP for unified access to trading data sources and tools.

A regulated bank chose an open harness on a managed model platform rather than a single-vendor agent product. The write-up is an AWS blog post, so read it as a reference architecture, not an independent evaluation.

evidence.title: Building trade assistant: How Jefferies optimized front office trading operations with AI

entries.title: Apollo rebuilds its GTM assistant on Deep Agents and LangSmith
entries.html:
Apollo rebuilt its AI Assistant on Deep Agents and LangSmith to cover the full go-to-market loop: prospecting, enrichment, outreach, analytics, and its own MCP integrations.

Together with Jefferies on Strands, it shows different harnesses reaching production in different industries; no single orchestration framework is winning outright. The case study is published by the framework vendor.

evidence.title: How Apollo Uses Deep Agents and LangSmith for GTM AI

also.title: Orchestration patterns: topologies, handoffs, and harnesses

entries.title: An A2A+MCP multi-agent system in a 5G-core SOC cuts detect and respond times 40%
entries.html:
A multi-agent architecture built on A2A and MCP in a live 5G-core security operations center targets the real bottleneck: keeping the detection rule base aligned with threats that evolve faster than rules get written, not analyst triage. It reports mean time to detect and respond down 40% and the human work required compressed 12x.

Coordination overhead can pay for itself in production when the task genuinely decomposes. The figures are the author's own.

evidence.title: Article: Multi-Agent AI for Production Security Operations: An A2A and MCP Architecture in a 5G Core

also.title: Orchestration patterns: topologies, handoffs, and harnesses

entries.title: Agora allocates sub-tasks to expert models and tools by auction
entries.html:
Agora replaces the coarse-grained matching a main agent uses to route sub-tasks with an incentive-compatible auction: candidate models and tools bid for each task, and allocation accounts for performance variability and cost among functionally similar options.

Fixed routing tables ignore exactly those differences. "Which agent handles this" becomes a market-clearing problem rather than a lookup.

evidence.title: Agora: Enhancing LLM Agent Reasoning Via Auction-Based Task Allocation

entries.title: In hierarchical search agents, which role gets the bigger model matters
entries.html:
"Think Big, Search Small" splits hierarchical search into a delegation role (task decomposition), an execution role (retrieval and evidence extraction), and an answer-generation role held fixed as a control. It then varies model capacity per role instead of running one model everywhere.

Capacity is not interchangeable between roles: the same topology can win or lose depending on which role gets the larger model. Size each role on purpose.

evidence.title: Think Big, Search Small: Where Capacity Matters in Hierarchical Search Agents?

entries.title: An arbiter agent settles planner-coder disagreements by checking code against the plan
entries.html:
In an InfoQ presentation, Itamar Friedman describes an arbiter role that resolves disagreement between a planning agent and a coding agent by checking the code against the plan, not trusting either agent's self-report. It only works when the plan is specified in enough detail to verify against.

He packages parallel testing, review, and context-retrieval agents plus the arbiter as a governance layer: distinct credentials per agent role and communication over human-readable channels such as GitHub or chat rather than hidden logs.

evidence.title: Presentation: The Multi-Agent Approach: Building Reliable and Controllable Software Development Automation

also.title: Orchestration patterns: topologies, handoffs, and harnesses

entries.title: Run Claude and Codex in parallel with a branch and sandbox each, then merge via a neutral verifier
entries.html:
A practitioner pattern gives each coding agent (Claude, Codex) its own git branch and sandboxed worktree, so no two agents touch the same branch and none can reach another's files. Work runs in frozen, read-only-reviewable rounds. Each candidate is replayed in a clean box by a neutral verifier, and the merge picks passing tests first, smallest diff second.

Isolation plus a control-flow gate, not smarter agents, keeps parallel agents from clobbering each other's work.

evidence.title: A Conflict-Free Multi-Agent Ensemble for Claude and Codex

entries.title: UA-ChatDev has role agents act on their own uncertainty to stop error propagation
entries.html:
UA-ChatDev targets hallucination propagation in role-based software-development agents. Existing frameworks treat every intermediate output as equally reliable, so a mistake made during requirements or design flows to every downstream role. UA-ChatDev's agents track their own confidence, and a low-confidence step triggers deliberation or a handoff instead of being passed on as fact.

Coordination reliability depends on agents knowing what they don't know, not only on topology.

evidence.title: UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development

entries.title: Multi-agent routers trust agents' self-descriptions; Linguistic Firewall defends that gap
entries.html:
Multi-agent routers decide which agent gets a task from unverified proxies: an agent's textual self-description or a static surrogate representation. The Linguistic Firewall paper treats the gap between an agent's projected profile and its actual competence as a security problem and proposes a geometry-based defense for routing.

The routing layer is an attack surface: an agent that misdescribes itself can capture work it should not get. Robust handoffs are a security property, not just a quality one.

evidence.title: Linguistic Firewall: Geometry as Defense in Multi-Agent Systems Routing

entries.title: Sakana Fugu delivers a multi-agent system as a single model
entries.html:
Sakana's Fugu collapses a multi-agent system into one model, trading the coordination layer away once the division of labor is known.

It is the far end of the "is it worth it" question: sometimes the cheapest topology is no topology at all. The cost is that you can no longer swap, inspect, or trace individual roles.

evidence.title: Sakana Fugu: a multi-agent system delivered as one model

entries.title: DPBench: communication structure, not agent count, decides whether coordination helps
entries.html:
DPBench studies the structural determinants of multi-agent LLM coordination: which topologies and role assignments make collaboration pay off and which only add noise. The communication structure comes out as the dominant variable.

Before adding agents, decide who talks to whom and in what format. That choice moves results more than the number of agents.

evidence.title: DPBench: Structural Determinants of Multi-Agent LLM Coordination

entries.title: Stanford's DeLM cuts multi-agent task cost ~50% by removing the central orchestrator
entries.html:
Stanford's DeLM reports cutting multi-agent task cost by roughly half by removing the central orchestrator.

A single coordinating agent is both a token bottleneck and a single point of failure. Decentralized topologies are harder to trace and can deadlock or diverge, so the saving comes with an observability bill. See agent cost.
